tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

schema.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Schedule
These deadlines can't move: TA check-in by **Nov 13**, app live by **Nov 20**, final submission on **Dec 1**. Here's a compressed plan that keeps all the required checks:

| Dates | Goal |
| --- | --- |
| Oct 30 – Nov 3 | Simulator (HH waveform, Poisson trains, recording), filter, detection, plus the detection checks |
| Nov 4 – 10 | Alignment, Haar, PCA, EM-GMM, BIC, scoring, ending in a first end-to-end sort |

| Nov 17 – 20 | Web app v1, deployed |
| Nov 21 – Dec 1 | Fixes, README, video, demo prep |

**Suggested cuts to fit this:**
- Start with Gaussian noise and add realistic background from distant neurons only if time allows.
- Drop the optional Trautmann extension.

Those are scope changes, so record them in CLAUDE.md or the README. For checkpoint 2 today, write an honest journal entry about where you are and this revised plan. Graders reward steady work, so it matters that the log shows you re-planning on purpose. Please also write your own update to the "Current status" line in CLAUDE.md.

## Lesson 1: Hodgkin–Huxley and the extracellular spike

**Why it matters:** each neuron's waveform shape is what the sorter uses to tell neurons apart, so the shape needs a physical basis.

**The model.** The membrane acts like a capacitor with three parallel current paths:

$$C\frac{dV}{dt} = I_{ext} - \bar g_{Na}\,m^3h\,(V-E_{Na}) - \bar g_K\,n^4\,(V-E_K) - g_L\,(V-E_L)$$

- **m** is the sodium activation gate. It is fast and opens when the cell depolarizes.
- **h** is the sodium inactivation gate. It is slow and closes when the cell depolarizes, which ends the sodium current.
- **n** is the potassium activation gate. It is slow and opens to bring V back down, which repolarizes the cell.

Each gate follows $\frac{dx}{dt} = \alpha_x(V)(1-x) - \beta_x(V)\,x$. Here α is the voltage-dependent rate at which closed gates open, and β is the rate at which open gates close. Together you get 4 coupled ODEs (V, m, h, n), and you'll integrate them with RK4.

**From inside the cell to the electrode.** The electrode doesn't measure V. It measures the potential that membrane current creates in the fluid around the cell. For a point source, $\phi \approx \frac{I_m}{4\pi\sigma r}$, where σ is the conductivity of the tissue fluid. During the upstroke, positive current flows *into* the cell, so the extracellular spike is **negative first**. Its shape looks roughly like −dV/dt or the summed ionic current, not like V.

**A subtlety we need to decide on (it may come up on Dec 3).** In a single-compartment model with no injected current, total membrane current sums to zero. Real extracellular spikes exist because current flows *in* at one part of the cell and *out* at another, which forms a dipole. A dipole falls off as **1/r²**, not 1/r. You have two options:
- Use the ionic current as the waveform shape and assume 1/r scaling. This is simple and common.
- Model it as a dipole with 1/r². This is more realistic.

Neither is wrong, but you'll need to state and justify whichever you pick.

## Your turn: explain these back to me
1. In your own words, what happens to m, h and n during one spike, in order?
2. Why is the extracellular spike negative first when the intracellular one goes positive first?
3. A neuron moves from 50 µm to 100 µm from the electrode. How much smaller is its spike under 1/r? Under 1/r²? Which law makes it harder to sort many neurons, and why?
4. Why use RK4 instead of Euler? What would you expect to see if Euler's time step were too large?

Answer in your own words, and wrong answers are fine. Once you've got these, we'll write the HH integrator. Its first check will be that a step current produces spikes at a sensible rate and resting potential.

- Set up the project folder with `git init` and a first commit, with the message written by you.

- Add `ROADMAP.md` with your plan.
- Write your checkpoint 2 journal entry, which is due today.

## Quiz feedback

**Q1: not right yet.** Several details are reversed:
- **m** opens fast when the cell depolarizes. It doesn't close right away; it only closes as V falls again.
- **h** is mostly *open* at rest and slowly *closes* during depolarization. It doesn't open and then close. Its closing is what shuts off the sodium current.
- **n** opens slowly and lets potassium out, which brings V back **down**, not up. Because n is slow to close again, V briefly dips below rest (the undershoot).

**Q2: correct.** One more step: inward current means current is *leaving* the fluid near that part of the membrane. That spot acts as a current "sink," which is why the nearby potential goes negative.

**Q3: you didn't answer the numbers part.** You also have a misconception about what 1/r and 1/r² mean:
- They aren't two parts of the action potential. They're two models of *where current enters and leaves the cell*.
- 1/r treats the cell as one point that current flows out of. In real cells, current goes in at one spot and comes out at another, which makes a dipole, so 1/r² is the more realistic model.

**Q4: mostly right.** To be more precise: for Euler, total error is proportional to dt. For RK4, it's proportional to dt⁴. So halving dt halves Euler's error but cuts RK4's error by 16×. You skipped the second half of the question.

**Please try again on these three:**
1. Retell Q1: what m, h and n each do during a spike, in order. Then add one more part: how do the slow gates cause a refractory period? (Your simulator uses about 2 ms.)
2. Q3 numbers: the neuron moves from 50 µm to 100 µm. By what factor does its spike shrink under 1/r, and under 1/r²? Using that, explain which law limits how many neurons the electrode can sort.
3. Q4 second half: what would you expect to see in your simulated V(t) if Euler's step were too large?

We can do the Week 0 setup first and come back to these before the HH integrator.

# 02-120 Project Proposal

Tara Prahlad

## 1. What is your scientific question?

How many distinct neurons can be reliably separated from a single electrode's signal, and how do waveform similarity, noise level and firing rate limit that number?

## 2. What will you build to answer it?

I want to build an interactive web app that will let me do two things:

a. **Simulate the firings of a neuron:** I want to make a recording simulator that will generate fake electrode data that looks like what a real electrode in the brain would record, except I would know which neuron caused each spike.

b. **Sort the spikes from each neuron:** I want to learn signal processing from this project so I'm thinking tentatively that it will include the following:

   1. Bandpass filtering
   2. Threshold detection with a robust noise estimate
   3. Peak alignment
   4. Haar wavelet features chosen by how non-Gaussian they are
   5. A Gaussian mixture model fitted by expectation-maximization

I'm thinking users can move sliders to adjust the noise level, number of neurons, waveform similarity and firing rate. The app will show the raw trace with sorted spikes colored, the feature space, each cluster's waveforms and accuracy against ground truth. A sweep view will plot how many neurons are recovered (after firing) as more added.

## 3. How will you check your model?

I will check my model with the following methods:

a. **Ground truth scoring:** detected spike will be matched to a true spike within a small time window.

b. **A detection rate that can be derived by hand:** the chance that one sample exceeds 4 standard deviations in either direction is 2(1 − Φ(4)) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻⁵ and the detector must match this on simulated noise.

c. **The robust noise estimate:** on pure noise, median(|x|) / 0.6745 must recover the true σ.

d. **A hand-solvable special case:** two neurons with very different waveforms and no noise need to be sorted properly.

e. **Component checks:** the Haar transform needs to invert exactly and EM must recover the known parameters of a synthetic Gaussian mixture.

f. **Published behavior:** wavelets need to match or beat PCA as sorting gets harder.

g. **Refractory violations:** correctly sorted units should almost never fire twice within 2 ms but merged units will.

If you have any questions, feel free to refer to this research paper: <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15228749/>

1	=== PAGE 1 ===
2	LETTER Communicated by Maneesh Sahani
3	Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting with Wavelets and
4	Superparamagnetic Clustering
5	R. Quian Quiroga
6	rodri@vis.caltech.edu
7	Z. Nadasdy
8	zoltan@vis.caltech.edu
9	Division of Biology, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, U.S.A.
10	Y. Ben-Shaul
11	ybss@md.huji.ac.il
12	ICNC, Hebrew University, Jerusalem, Israel
13	This study introduces a new method for detecting and sorting spikes from
14	multiunit recordings. The method combines the wavelet transform, which
15	localizes distinctive spike features, with superparamagnetic clustering,
16	which allows automatic classification of the data without assumptions
17	such as low variance or gaussian distributions. Moreover, an improved
18	method for setting amplitude thresholds for spike detection is proposed.
19	We describe several criteria for implementation that render the algorithm
20	unsupervised and fast. The algorithm is compared to other conventional
21	methods using several simulated data sets whose characteristics closely
22	resemble those of in vivo recordings. For these data sets, we found that
23	the proposed algorithm outperformed conventional methods.
24	1 Introduction
25	Many questions in neuroscience depend on the analysis of neuronal spik-
26	ing activity recorded under various behavioral conditions. For this reason,
27	data acquired simultaneously from multiple neurons are invaluable for elu-
28	cidating principles of neural information processing. Recent advances in
29	commercially available acquisition systems allow recordings of up to hun-
30	dreds of channels simultaneously, and the reliability of these data criti-
31	cally depends on accurately identifying the activity of individual neurons.
32	However, developments of efficient and reliable computational methods
33	for classifying multiunit data, that is, spike sorting algorithms, lag behind
34	the capabilities afforded by current hardware. In practice, supervised spike
35	sorting of a large number of channels is highly time-consuming and nearly
36	impossible to perform during the course of an experiment.
37	Neural Computation 16, 1661–1687 (2004) c ⃝ 2004 Massachusetts Institute of Technology
38	=== PAGE 2 ===
39	1662 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
40	The basic algorithmic steps of spike classification are as follows: (1) spike
41	detection, (2) extraction of distinctive features from the spike shapes, and
42	(3) clustering of the spikes by these features. Spike sorting methods are
43	typically based on clustering predefined spike shape features such as peak-
44	to-peak amplitude, width, or principal components (Abeles & Goldstein,
45	1977; Lewicki, 1998). Nevertheless, it is impossible to know beforehand
46	which of these features is optimal for discriminating between spike classes
47	in a given data set. In the specific case where the spike features are projec-
48	tions on the first few principal components, the planes onto which the spikes
49	are projected maximize the variance of data but do not necessarily provide
50	an optimal separation between the clusters. A second critical issue is that
51	even when optimal features from a given data set are used for classification,
52	the distribution of the data imposes additional constraints on the clustering
53	procedure. In particular, violation of normality in a given feature’s distribu-
54	tion compromises most unsupervised clustering algorithms, and therefore
55	manual clustering of the data is usually preferred. However, besides being a
56	very time-consuming task, manual clustering introduces errors due to both
57	the limited dimensionality of the cluster cutting space and human biases
58	(Harris, Henze, Csicsvari, Hirase, & Buzs´ aki, 2000). An alternative approach
59	is to define spike classes by a set of manually selected thresholds (window
60	discriminators) or with spike templates. Although this is computationally
61	very efficient and can be implemented on-line, it is reliable only when the
62	signal-to-noise ratio is very high and it is limited to the number of channels
63	a human operator is able to supervise.
64	In this article, we introduce a new method that improves spike separa-
65	tion in the feature space and implements a novel unsupervised clustering
66	algorithm. Combining these two features results in a novel unsupervised
67	spike sorting system. The cornerstones of our method are the wavelet trans-
68	form, which is a time-frequency decomposition of the signal with optimal
69	resolution in both the time and the frequency domains, and superparam-
70	agnetic clustering (SPC; Blatt, Wiseman, & Domany, 1996), a relatively new
71	clustering procedure developed in the context of statistical mechanics. The
72	complete algorithm encompasses three principal stages: (1) spike detec-
73	tion, (2) selection of spike features, and (3) clustering of the selected spike
74	features.
75	In the first step, spikes are detected with an automatic amplitude thresh-
76	old on the high-pass filtered data. In the second step, a small set of wavelet
77	coefficients from each spike is chosen as input for the clustering algorithm.
78	Finally, the SPC classifies the spikes according to the selected set of wavelet
79	coefficients. We stress that the entire process of detection, feature extraction,
80	and clustering is performed without supervision and relatively quickly. In
81	this study, we compare the performance of the algorithm with other meth-
82	ods using simulated data that closely resemble real recordings. The rationale
83	of using simulated data is to obtain an objective measure of performance,
84	since the simulation sets the identity of the spikes.
85	=== PAGE 3 ===
86	1663
87	(2.1)
88	Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 2 Theoretical Background
89	2.1 Wavelet Transform. The wavelet transform (WT) is a time-frequency
90	representation of the signal that has two main advantages over conven-
91	tional methods: it provides an optimal resolution in both the time and the
92	frequency domains, and it eliminates the requirement of signal stationar-
93	ity. It is defined as the convolution between the signal x(t) and the wavelet
94	functions ψa,b(t),
95	Wψ X(a, b) = ⟨x(t) | ψa,b(t)⟩, where ψa,b(t) are dilated (contracted), and shifted versions of a unique
96	wavelet function ψ(t),

98	ψa,b(t) = |a|−
99	2 ψ
100	t− b
101	a
102	(2.2)
103	where a and b are the scale and translation parameters, respectively. Equa-
104	tion 2.1 can be inverted, thus providing the reconstruction of x(t).
105	The WT maps the signal that is represented by one independent variable
106	t onto a function of two independent variables a, b. This procedure is redun-
107	dant and inefficient for algorithmic implementations; therefore, the WT is
108	usually defined at discrete scales a and discrete times b by choosing the set
109	of parameters {aj= 2−j; bj,k = 2−jk}, with integers j and k. Contracted ver-
110	sions of the wavelet function match the high-frequency components, while
111	dilated versions match the low-frequency components. Then, by correlating
112	the original signal with wavelet functions of different sizes, we can obtain
113	details of the signal at several scales. These correlations with the different
114	wavelet functions can be arranged in a hierarchical scheme called multires-
115	olution decomposition (Mallat, 1989). The multiresolution decomposition
116	algorithm separates the signal into details at different scales and a coarser
117	representation of the signal named “approximation” (for details, see Mallat,
118	1989; Chui, 1992; Samar, Swartz, & Raghveer, 1995; Quian Quiroga, Sakow-
119	icz, Basar, & Sch ¨ urmann, 2001; Quian Quiroga & Garcia, 2003).
120	In this study we implemented a four-level decomposition using Haar
121	wavelets, which are rescaled square functions. Haar wavelets were chosen
122	due to their compact support and orthogonality, which allows the discrimi-
123	native features of the spikes to be expressed with a few wavelet coefficients
124	and without a priori assumptions on the spike shapes.
125	2.2 Superparamagnetic Clustering. The following is a brief description
126	of the key ideas of superparamagnetic clustering (SPC), which is based on
127	simulated interactions between each data point and its K-nearest neighbors
128	(for details, see Blatt et al., 1996; Blatt, Wiseman, & Domany, 1997). The
129	method is implemented as a Monte Carlo iteration of a Potts model. The
130	=== PAGE 4 ===
131	1664 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
132	Potts model is a generalization of the Ising model where instead of having
133	spins with values ±1/2, there are q different states per particle (Binder &
134	Heermann, 1988).
135	The first step is to represent the m selected features of each spike i by a
136	point xi in an m-dimensional phase space. The interaction strength between
137	points xi is then defined as
138	Jij=
139	    

141	K exp−

146	where a is the average nearest-neighbors distance and K is the number of
147	nearest neighbors. Note that the strength of interaction Jij between nearest-
148	neighbor spikes falls off exponentially with increasing Euclidean distance
149	dij = ∥xi− xj∥2, which corresponds to the similarity of the selected features
150	(i.e., similar spikes will have a strong interaction).
151	In the second step, an initial random state s from 1 to q is assigned to each
152	point xi. Then N Monte Carlo iterations are run for different temperatures T
153	using the Wolf algorithm (Wolf, 1989; Binder & Heermann, 1988). Blatt et al.
154	(1997) used a Swendnsen-Wang algorithm instead, but its implementation
155	and performance are both very similar. The advantage of both algorithms
156	over simpler approaches such as the Metropolis algorithm is their enhanced
157	performance in the superparamagnetic regime (see Binder & Heermann,
158	1988; Blatt et al., 1997, for details). The main idea of the Wolf algorithm is
159	that given an initial configuration of states s, a point xi is randomly selected
160	and its state s changed to a new state snew, randomly chosen between 1 and
161	q. The probability that the nearest neighbors of xi will also change their state
162	to snew is given by
163	pij= 1− exp−

166	where T is the temperature (see below). Note that only those nearest neigh-
167	bors of xi that were in the same previous state s are the candidates to change
168	their values to snew. Neighbors that change their values create a “frontier”
169	and cannot change their value again during the same iteration. Points that
170	do not change their value in a first attempt can do so if revisited during the
171	same iteration. Then for each point of the frontier, we apply equation 2.4
172	again to calculate the probability of changing the state to snew for their re-
173	spective neighbors. The frontier is updated, and the update is repeated until
174	the frontier does not change any more. At that stage, we start the procedure
175	again from another point and repeat it several times in order to get represen-
176	tative statistics. Points that are relatively close together (i.e., corresponding
177	to a given cluster) will change their state together. This observation can be
178	quantified by measuring the point-point correlation ⟨δsi,sj ⟩ and defining xi,
179	xj to be members of the same cluster if ⟨δsi,sj ⟩ ≥ θ , for a given threshold θ.
180	Jij
181	=== PAGE 5 ===
182	Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 1665
183	As in Blatt et al. (1996), we used q= 20 states, K= 11 nearest neighbors,
184	N= 500 iterations, and θ= 0.5. It has indeed been shown that clustering
185	results mainly depend on the temperature and are robust to small changes
186	in the previous parameters (Blatt et al., 1996).
187	Let us now discuss the role of the temperature T. Note from equation 2.4
188	that high temperatures correspond to a low probability of changing the state
189	of neighboring points together, whereas low temperatures correspond to a
190	higher probability regardless of how weak the interaction Jij is. This has a
191	physical analogy with a spin glass, in which at a relatively high temperature,
192	all the spins are switching randomly, regardless of their interactions (para-
193	magnetic phase). At a low temperature, the entire spin glass changes its
194	state together (ferromagnetic phase). However, at a certain medium range
195	of temperatures, the system reaches a “superparamagnetic” phase in which
196	only those spins that are grouped together will change their state simulta-
197	neously. Regarding our clustering problem, at low temperatures, all points
198	will change their state together and will therefore be considered as a single
199	cluster; at high temperatures, many points will change their state indepen-
200	dently from one another, thus partitioning the data into several clusters
201	with only a few points in each; and for temperatures corresponding to the
202	superparamagnetic phase, only those points that are grouped together will
203	change their state simultaneously.
204	Figure 1A shows a two-dimensional (2D) example in which 2400 2D
205	points were distributed in three different clusters. Note that the clusters
206	partially overlap, they have a large variance, and, moreover, the centers fall
207	outside the clusters. In particular, the distance between arbitrarily chosen
208	points of the same cluster can be much larger than the distance between
209	points in different clusters. These features render the use of conventional
210	clustering algorithms unreliable. The different markers represent the out-
211	come after clustering with SPC. Clearly, most of the points were correctly
212	classified. In fact, only 102 of 2400 (4%) data points were not classified be-
213	cause they were near the boundaries of the clusters. Figure 1B shows the
214	number of elements assigned to each given cluster as a function of the tem-
215	perature. At low temperatures, we have a single cluster with all 2400 data
216	points included. At a temperature between 0.04 and 0.05, this cluster breaks
217	down into three subclusters corresponding to the superparamagnetic transi-
218	tion. The classification shown in the upper plot was performed at T= 0.05.
219	At about T= 0.08, we observe the transition to the paramagnetic phase,
220	where the clusters break down into several groups with a few members each.
221	Note that the algorithm is based on K-nearest neighbor interactions and
222	therefore does not assume that clusters are nonoverlapping or that they
223	have low variance or a gaussian distribution.
224	3 Description of the Method
225	Figure 2 summarizes the three principal stages of the algorithm: (1) spikes
226	are detected automatically via amplitude thresholding; (2) the wavelet trans-
227	=== PAGE 6 ===
228	1666 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
229	Figure 1: Example showing the performance of superparamagnetic clustering.
230	(A) The two-dimensional data points used as inputs. The different markers rep-
231	resent the outcome of the clustering algorithm. (B) Cluster size vs. temperature.
232	At temperature 0.05, the transition to the superparamagnetic phase occurs, and
233	the three clusters are separated.
234	form is calculated for each of the spikes and the optimal coefficients for
235	separating the spike classes are automatically selected; and (3) the selected
236	wavelet coefficients then serve as the input to the SPC algorithm, and cluster-
237	ing is performed after automatic selection of the temperature corresponding
238	to the superparamagnetic phase. (A Matlab implementation of the algorithm
239	can be obtained on-line from www.vis.caltech.edu/∼rodri.)
240	3.1 Spike Detection. Spike detection was performed by amplitude
241	thresholding after bandpass filtering the signal (300–6000 Hz, four pole

243	Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 1667
244	Figure 2: Overview of the automatic clustering procedure. (A) Spikes are de-
245	tected by setting an amplitude threshold. (B) A set of wavelet coefficients rep-
246	resenting the relevant features of the spikes is selected. (C) The SPC algorithm
247	is used to cluster the spikes automatically.
248	=== PAGE 8 ===
249	1668 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
250	butterworth filter). The threshold (Thr) was automatically set to
251	Thr= 4σn; σn = median |x|
252	0.6745, (3.1)
253	where x is the bandpass-filtered signal and σn is an estimate of the stan-
254	dard deviation of the background noise (Donoho & Johnstone, 1994). Note
255	that taking the standard deviation of the signal (including the spikes) could
256	lead to very high threshold values, especially in cases with high firing rates
257	and large spike amplitudes. In contrast, by using the estimation based on
258	the median, the interference of the spikes is diminished (under the reason-
259	able assumption that spikes amount to a small fraction of all samples). To
260	demonstrate this, we generated a segment of 10 sec of background noise
261	with unit standard deviation, and in successive simulations, we added a
262	distinct spike class with different firing rates. Figure 3 shows that for noise
263	alone (i.e., zero firing rate), both estimates are equal, but as the firing rate
264	increases, the standard deviation of the signal (conventional estimate) gives
265	an increasingly erroneous estimate of the noise level, whereas the improved
266	estimate from equation 3.1 remains close to the real value.
267	For each detected spike, 64 samples (i.e.,∼2.5 ms) were saved for further
268	analysis. All spikes were aligned to their maximum at data point 20. In
269	order to avoid spike misalignments due to low sampling, spike maxima
270	were determined from interpolated waveforms of 256 samples, using cubic
271	splines.
272	3.2 Selection of Wavelet Coefficients. After spikes are detected, their
273	wavelet transform is calculated, thus obtaining 64 wavelet coefficients for
274	each spike. We implemented a four-level multiresolution decomposition
275	using Haar wavelets. As explained in section 2.1, each wavelet coefficient
276	characterizes the spike shapes at different scales and times. The goal is to
277	select a few coefficients that best separate the different spike classes. Clearly,
278	such coefficients should have a multimodal distribution (unless there is
279	only one spike class). To perform this selection automatically, the Lilliefors
280	modification of a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test for normality was used
281	(Press, Teukolsky, Vetterling, & Flannery, 1992). Note that we do not rely on
282	any particular distribution of the data; rather, we are interested in deviation
283	from normality as a sign of a multimodal distribution. Given a data set x, the
284	test compares the cumulative distribution function of the data (F(x)) with
285	that of a gaussian distribution with the same mean and variance (G(x)).
286	Deviation from normality is then quantified by
287	max(|F(x)− G(x)|). (3.2)
288	In our implementation, the first 10 coefficients with the largest deviation
289	from normality were used. The selected set of wavelet coefficients provides

321	3.3 SPC and Localization of the Superparamagnetic Phase. Once the
322	selected set of wavelet coefficients is chosen, we run the SPC algorithm for
323	a wide range of temperatures spanning the ferromagnetic, superparamag-
324	=== PAGE 10 ===
325	1670 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
326	netic, and paramagnetic phases. In order to localize the superparamagnetic
327	phase automatically, a criterion based on the cluster sizes is used. The idea
328	is that for both the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases, temperature in-
329	creases can only lead to the creation of clusters with few members each. In-
330	deed, in the paramagnetic phase (i.e., high temperature), the clusters break
331	down into several small ones, and in the ferromagnetic phase, there are
332	almost no changes when the temperature is increased. In contrast, in the
333	superparamagnetic phase, increasing the temperature creates new clusters
334	with a large number of members.
335	In our implementation, we varied the temperature from 0 to 0.2 in in-
336	crements of 0.01 and looked for the highest temperature at which a clus-
337	ter containing more than 60 points appeared (not being present at lower
338	temperatures). Since our simulations were 60 sec long, this means that we
339	considered clusters corresponding to neurons with a mean firing rate of at
340	least 1 Hz. The threshold of 1 Hz gave us optimal results for all our sim-
341	ulations, but it should be decreased if one considers neurons with lower
342	firing rates. Alternatively, one can consider a fraction of the total number
343	of spikes. If no cluster with a minimum of 60 points was found, we kept
344	the minimum temperature value. Using this criterion, we can automatically
345	select the optimal temperature for cluster assignments, and therefore the
346	whole clustering procedure becomes unsupervised.
347	4 Data Simulation
348	Simulated signals were constructed using a database of 594 different av-
349	erage spike shapes compiled from recordings in the neocortex and basal
350	ganglia. For generating background noise, spikes randomly selected from
351	the database were superimposed at random times and amplitudes. This was
352	done for half the times of the samples. The rationale was to mimic the back-
353	ground noise of actual recordings that is generated by the activity of distant
354	neurons. Next, we superimposed a train of three distinct spike shapes (also
355	preselected from the same database of spikes) on the noise signal at random
356	times. The amplitude of the three spike classes was normalized to have a
357	peak value of 1. The noise level was determined from its standard deviation,
358	which was equal to 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2 relative to the amplitude of the
359	spike classes. In one case, since clustering was relatively easy, we also con-
360	sidered noise levels 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, and 0.4. Spike times and identities were
361	saved for subsequent evaluation of the clustering algorithm. The data were
362	first simulated at a sampling rate of 96,000 Hz, and by using interpolated
363	waveforms of the original spike shapes, we simulated the spike times to
364	fall continuously between samples (to machine precision). Finally, the data
365	were downsampled to 24,000 Hz. This procedure was introduced in order
366	to imitate actual recording conditions in which samples do not necessarily
367	fall on the same features within a spike (i.e., the peak of the signal does not
368	necessarily coincide with a discrete sample).
369	=== PAGE 11 ===
370	Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 1671

375	Mitra, & Kleinfeld, 1996; Pouzat, Mazor, & Laurent, 2002). Moreover, con-

850	5.4 Comparison with Other Spike Features. Errors of spike identifi-
851	cation cumulatively derive from two sources: incorrect feature extraction
852	and incorrect clustering. First, we compared the discrimination power of
853	wavelets at different noise levels with other feature extraction methods us-
854	ing the same clustering algorithm, SPC. Specifically, we compared the out-
855	come of classification with wavelets, principal component analysis (using
856	the first three principal components), the whole spike shape, and a fixed set
857	of spike features. The spike features were the mean square value of the sig-
858	nal (energy), the amplitude of the main peak, and the amplitude of the peaks
859	preceding and following it. The width of the spike (given by the position of
860	the three peaks) was also tested but found to worsen the spike classification.
861	Table 2 summarizes the results (examples 1 and 2 were shown in Figures 4
862	and 5, respectively). Performance was quantified in terms of the number of
863	classification errors and the number of clusters detected. Values in brackets
864	denote the number of clusters detected, when different from 3. Errors due
865	to overlapping spikes are not included in the table (but overlapping spikes
866	were also inputs to the algorithm). Since example 1 was easier to cluster, in
867	this case we also analyzed four higher noise levels.
868	In general, the best performance was achieved using the selected wavelet
869	coefficients as spike features. In fact, with wavelets, all three clusters are
870	correctly detected, with the exception of example 4, noise level 0.2. Using
871	the other features, only one cluster is detected when increasing the noise
872	level. Considering all wavelet coefficients as inputs to SPC (i.e., without the
873	selection based on the KS test) gave nearly the same results as those ob-
874	tained using the entire spike shape (not shown). This is not surprising since
875	the wavelet transform is linear, which implies rotations or rescaling of the
876	original high-dimensional space. The clear benefit is introduced when con-
877	sidering only those coefficients that allow a good separation between the
878	clusters, using the KS test. Note that PCA features gave slightly worse re-
879	sults than those using the entire spike shapes (and clearly worse than using
880	wavelets). Therefore, PCA gives a reasonable solution when using clustering
881	algorithms that cannot handle high-dimensional spaces (although this is not
882	a problem for SPC). The fixed features, such as peak amplitudes and mean
883	squared values, were much less efficient. This was expected since spike
884	classes were generated with the same peak value and in some cases also
885	with very similar shapes that could not be discriminated by these features.
886	We remark that the number of detected clusters decreases monotonically
887	with noise level, but the number of classification errors does not necessarily
888	increase monotonically because even when three clusters are correctly rec-
889	ognized, a large number of spikes may remain unassigned to any of them
890	(see, e.g., example 4 with PCA for noise levels 0.05 and 0.1).

953	6 Discussion
954	We presented a method for detection and sorting neuronal multiunit activ-
955	ity. The procedure is fully unsupervised and fast, thus being particularly
956	interesting for the classification of spikes from a large number of channels
957	recorded simultaneously. To obtain a quantitative measure of its perfor-
958	mance, the method was tested on simulated data sets with different noise
959	levels and similar spike shapes. The noise was generated by superposition of
960	a large number of small-amplitude spikes, resembling characteristics of real
961	recordings. This makes the spectral characteristics of noise and spikes simi-
962	lar, thus increasing the difficulty in detection and clustering. The proposed
963	method had an overall better performance than conventional approaches,
964	such as using PCA for extracting spike features or K-means for clustering.
965	Spike detection was achieved by using an amplitude threshold on the
966	high-pass filtered data. The threshold value was calculated automatically
967	using the median of the absolute value of the signal. The advantage of this
968	estimation, rather than using the variance of the overall signal, is that it
969	diminishes the dependence of the threshold on the firing rate and the peak-
970	to-peak amplitude of the spikes, thus giving an improved estimation of the
971	background noise level. Indeed, high firing rates and high spike amplitudes
972	lead to an overestimation of the appropriate threshold value. In terms of the
973	number of misses and number of false positives, the proposed automatic
974	detection procedure had good performance for the different examples and
975	noise levels.
976	The advantage of using the wavelet transform as a feature extractor is that
977	very localized shape differences of the different units can be discerned. The
978	information about the shape of the spikes is distributed in several wavelet
979	coefficients, whereas with PCA, most of the information about the spike
980	shapes is captured only by the first three principal components (Letelier

982	lata, Segev, & Ben-Jacob, 2002), which are not necessarily optimal for cluster

984	in time. In agreement with these considerations, a better performance of
985	=== PAGE 24 ===
986	1684 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
987	wavelet coefficients in comparison with PCA was shown for several exam-
988	ples generated with different noise levels. For comparison, we also used the
989	whole spike shape as input to the clustering algorithm. As shown in Table
990	2, the dimensionality reduction achieved with the KS test clearly improves
991	the clustering performance. Since wavelets are a linear transform, using all
992	the wavelet coefficients yields nearly the same results as taking the entire
993	spike shape (as it is just a rescaling of the space). Since the need of a low-
994	dimensional space is a limiting factor for many clustering algorithms, the
995	dimensionality reduction achieved by combining wavelets with the KS test
996	may have a broad range of interest.
997	The use of wavelets for spike sorting has been proposed recently by Lete-
998	lier et al. (2000) and Hulata et al. (2000, 2002). Our approach differs from
999	theirs in several aspects, most notably by the implementation of our algo-
1000	rithm as a single unsupervised process. One key feature of our algorithm
1001	is the choice of wavelet coefficients by using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of
1002	normality, thus selecting features that give an optimal separation between
1003	the different clusters. Letelier et al. (2000) suggested to visually select those
1004	wavelet coefficients with the largest mean, variance, and, most fundamen-
1005	tal, multimodal distribution. However, neither a large average nor a large
1006	variance entitles the given coefficient to be the best separator. In contrast, we
1007	considered only the multimodality of the distributions. In this respect, we
1008	showed that coefficients in the low-frequency bands, with a large variance
1009	and uniform distribution, are not appropriate for the separation of distinct
1010	clusters. In contrast, they introduce dimensions with nonsegregated distri-
1011	butions that in practice may compromise the performance of the clustering
1012	algorithm. A caveat of the KS test as an estimator of multimodality is that it
1013	can also select unimodal nongaussian distributions (those that are skewed
1014	or have large kurtosis). In fact, this was the case of three coefficients shown
1015	in Figure 7. Despite this limitation, the selection of wavelet coefficients with
1016	the KS test gave optimal results that indeed outperformed other feature
1017	selection methods.

1019	variance of the data are selected, but these directions do not necessarily pro-
1020	vide the best separation of the spike classes. In other words, it may well be

1040	gaussian). Superparamagnetic clustering has already been applied with ex-

=== PAGE 1 ===
LETTER Communicated by Maneesh Sahani
Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting with Wavelets and
Superparamagnetic Clustering
R. Quian Quiroga
rodri@vis.caltech.edu
Z. Nadasdy
zoltan@vis.caltech.edu
Division of Biology, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, U.S.A.
Y. Ben-Shaul
ybss@md.huji.ac.il
ICNC, Hebrew University, Jerusalem, Israel
This study introduces a new method for detecting and sorting spikes from
multiunit recordings. The method combines the wavelet transform, which
localizes distinctive spike features, with superparamagnetic clustering,
which allows automatic classification of the data without assumptions
such as low variance or gaussian distributions. Moreover, an improved
method for setting amplitude thresholds for spike detection is proposed.
We describe several criteria for implementation that render the algorithm
unsupervised and fast. The algorithm is compared to other conventional
methods using several simulated data sets whose characteristics closely
resemble those of in vivo recordings. For these data sets, we found that
the proposed algorithm outperformed conventional methods.
1 Introduction
Many questions in neuroscience depend on the analysis of neuronal spik-
ing activity recorded under various behavioral conditions. For this reason,
data acquired simultaneously from multiple neurons are invaluable for elu-
cidating principles of neural information processing. Recent advances in
commercially available acquisition systems allow recordings of up to hun-
dreds of channels simultaneously, and the reliability of these data criti-
cally depends on accurately identifying the activity of individual neurons.
However, developments of efficient and reliable computational methods
for classifying multiunit data, that is, spike sorting algorithms, lag behind
the capabilities afforded by current hardware. In practice, supervised spike
sorting of a large number of channels is highly time-consuming and nearly
impossible to perform during the course of an experiment.
Neural Computation 16, 1661–1687 (2004) c ⃝ 2004 Massachusetts Institute of Technology
=== PAGE 2 ===
1662 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
The basic algorithmic steps of spike classification are as follows: (1) spike
detection, (2) extraction of distinctive features from the spike shapes, and
(3) clustering of the spikes by these features. Spike sorting methods are
typically based on clustering predefined spike shape features such as peak-
to-peak amplitude, width, or principal components (Abeles & Goldstein,
1977; Lewicki, 1998). Nevertheless, it is impossible to know beforehand
which of these features is optimal for discriminating between spike classes
in a given data set. In the specific case where the spike features are projec-
tions on the first few principal components, the planes onto which the spikes
are projected maximize the variance of data but do not necessarily provide
an optimal separation between the clusters. A second critical issue is that
even when optimal features from a given data set are used for classification,
the distribution of the data imposes additional constraints on the clustering
procedure. In particular, violation of normality in a given feature’s distribu-
tion compromises most unsupervised clustering algorithms, and therefore
manual clustering of the data is usually preferred. However, besides being a
very time-consuming task, manual clustering introduces errors due to both
the limited dimensionality of the cluster cutting space and human biases
(Harris, Henze, Csicsvari, Hirase, & Buzs´ aki, 2000). An alternative approach
is to define spike classes by a set of manually selected thresholds (window
discriminators) or with spike templates. Although this is computationally
very efficient and can be implemented on-line, it is reliable only when the
signal-to-noise ratio is very high and it is limited to the number of channels
a human operator is able to supervise.
In this article, we introduce a new method that improves spike separa-
tion in the feature space and implements a novel unsupervised clustering
algorithm. Combining these two features results in a novel unsupervised
spike sorting system. The cornerstones of our method are the wavelet trans-
form, which is a time-frequency decomposition of the signal with optimal
resolution in both the time and the frequency domains, and superparam-
agnetic clustering (SPC; Blatt, Wiseman, & Domany, 1996), a relatively new
clustering procedure developed in the context of statistical mechanics. The
complete algorithm encompasses three principal stages: (1) spike detec-
tion, (2) selection of spike features, and (3) clustering of the selected spike
features.
In the first step, spikes are detected with an automatic amplitude thresh-
old on the high-pass filtered data. In the second step, a small set of wavelet
coefficients from each spike is chosen as input for the clustering algorithm.
Finally, the SPC classifies the spikes according to the selected set of wavelet
coefficients. We stress that the entire process of detection, feature extraction,
and clustering is performed without supervision and relatively quickly. In
this study, we compare the performance of the algorithm with other meth-
ods using simulated data that closely resemble real recordings. The rationale
of using simulated data is to obtain an objective measure of performance,
since the simulation sets the identity of the spikes.
=== PAGE 3 ===
1663
(2.1)
Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 2 Theoretical Background
2.1 Wavelet Transform. The wavelet transform (WT) is a time-frequency
representation of the signal that has two main advantages over conven-
tional methods: it provides an optimal resolution in both the time and the
frequency domains, and it eliminates the requirement of signal stationar-
ity. It is defined as the convolution between the signal x(t) and the wavelet
functions ψa,b(t),
Wψ X(a, b) = ⟨x(t) | ψa,b(t)⟩, where ψa,b(t) are dilated (contracted), and shifted versions of a unique
wavelet function ψ(t),
1

(2.2)
where a and b are the scale and translation parameters, respectively. Equa-
tion 2.1 can be inverted, thus providing the reconstruction of x(t).
The WT maps the signal that is represented by one independent variable
t onto a function of two independent variables a, b. This procedure is redun-
dant and inefficient for algorithmic implementations; therefore, the WT is
usually defined at discrete scales a and discrete times b by choosing the set
of parameters {aj= 2−j; bj,k = 2−jk}, with integers j and k. Contracted ver-
sions of the wavelet function match the high-frequency components, while
dilated versions match the low-frequency components. Then, by correlating
the original signal with wavelet functions of different sizes, we can obtain
details of the signal at several scales. These correlations with the different
wavelet functions can be arranged in a hierarchical scheme called multires-
olution decomposition (Mallat, 1989). The multiresolution decomposition
algorithm separates the signal into details at different scales and a coarser
representation of the signal named “approximation” (for details, see Mallat,
1989; Chui, 1992; Samar, Swartz, & Raghveer, 1995; Quian Quiroga, Sakow-
icz, Basar, & Sch ¨ urmann, 2001; Quian Quiroga & Garcia, 2003).
In this study we implemented a four-level decomposition using Haar
wavelets, which are rescaled square functions. Haar wavelets were chosen
due to their compact support and orthogonality, which allows the discrimi-
native features of the spikes to be expressed with a few wavelet coefficients
and without a priori assumptions on the spike shapes.
2.2 Superparamagnetic Clustering. The following is a brief description
of the key ideas of superparamagnetic clustering (SPC), which is based on
simulated interactions between each data point and its K-nearest neighbors
(for details, see Blatt et al., 1996; Blatt, Wiseman, & Domany, 1997). The
method is implemented as a Monte Carlo iteration of a Potts model. The
=== PAGE 4 ===
1664 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
Potts model is a generalization of the Ising model where instead of having
spins with values ±1/2, there are q different states per particle (Binder &
Heermann, 1988).
The first step is to represent the m selected features of each spike i by a
point xi in an m-dimensional phase space. The interaction strength between
points xi is then defined as
Jij=

where a is the average nearest-neighbors distance and K is the number of
nearest neighbors. Note that the strength of interaction Jij between nearest-
neighbor spikes falls off exponentially with increasing Euclidean distance
dij = ∥xi− xj∥2, which corresponds to the similarity of the selected features
(i.e., similar spikes will have a strong interaction).
In the second step, an initial random state s from 1 to q is assigned to each
point xi. Then N Monte Carlo iterations are run for different temperatures T
using the Wolf algorithm (Wolf, 1989; Binder & Heermann, 1988). Blatt et al.
(1997) used a Swendnsen-Wang algorithm instead, but its implementation
and performance are both very similar. The advantage of both algorithms
over simpler approaches such as the Metropolis algorithm is their enhanced
performance in the superparamagnetic regime (see Binder & Heermann,
1988; Blatt et al., 1997, for details). The main idea of the Wolf algorithm is
that given an initial configuration of states s, a point xi is randomly selected
and its state s changed to a new state snew, randomly chosen between 1 and
q. The probability that the nearest neighbors of xi will also change their state
to snew is given by

where T is the temperature (see below). Note that only those nearest neigh-
bors of xi that were in the same previous state s are the candidates to change
their values to snew. Neighbors that change their values create a “frontier”
and cannot change their value again during the same iteration. Points that
do not change their value in a first attempt can do so if revisited during the
same iteration. Then for each point of the frontier, we apply equation 2.4
again to calculate the probability of changing the state to snew for their re-
spective neighbors. The frontier is updated, and the update is repeated until
the frontier does not change any more. At that stage, we start the procedure
again from another point and repeat it several times in order to get represen-
tative statistics. Points that are relatively close together (i.e., corresponding
to a given cluster) will change their state together. This observation can be
quantified by measuring the point-point correlation ⟨δsi,sj ⟩ and defining xi,
xj to be members of the same cluster if ⟨δsi,sj ⟩ ≥ θ , for a given threshold θ.

=== PAGE 5 ===
Unsupervised Spike Detection and Sorting 1665
As in Blatt et al. (1996), we used q= 20 states, K= 11 nearest neighbors,
N= 500 iterations, and θ= 0.5. It has indeed been shown that clustering
results mainly depend on the temperature and are robust to small changes
in the previous parameters (Blatt et al., 1996).
Let us now discuss the role of the temperature T. Note from equation 2.4
that high temperatures correspond to a low probability of changing the state
of neighboring points together, whereas low temperatures correspond to a
higher probability regardless of how weak the interaction Jij is. This has a
physical analogy with a spin glass, in which at a relatively high temperature,
all the spins are switching randomly, regardless of their interactions (para-
magnetic phase). At a low temperature, the entire spin glass changes its
state together (ferromagnetic phase). However, at a certain medium range
of temperatures, the system reaches a “superparamagnetic” phase in which
only those spins that are grouped together will change their state simulta-
neously. Regarding our clustering problem, at low temperatures, all points
will change their state together and will therefore be considered as a single
cluster; at high temperatures, many points will change their state indepen-
dently from one another, thus partitioning the data into several clusters
with only a few points in each; and for temperatures corresponding to the
superparamagnetic phase, only those points that are grouped together will
change their state simultaneously.
Figure 1A shows a two-dimensional (2D) example in which 2400 2D
points were distributed in three different clusters. Note that the clusters
partially overlap, they have a large variance, and, moreover, the centers fall
outside the clusters. In particular, the distance between arbitrarily chosen
points of the same cluster can be much larger than the distance between
points in different clusters. These features render the use of conventional
clustering algorithms unreliable. The different markers represent the out-
come after clustering with SPC. Clearly, most of the points were correctly
classified. In fact, only 102 of 2400 (4%) data points were not classified be-
cause they were near the boundaries of the clusters. Figure 1B shows the
number of elements assigned to each given cluster as a function of the tem-
perature. At low temperatures, we have a single cluster with all 2400 data
points included. At a temperature between 0.04 and 0.05, this cluster breaks
down into three subclusters corresponding to the superparamagnetic transi-
tion. The classification shown in the upper plot was performed at T= 0.05.
At about T= 0.08, we observe the transition to the paramagnetic phase,
where the clusters break down into several groups with a few members each.
Note that the algorithm is based on K-nearest neighbor interactions and
therefore does not assume that clusters are nonoverlapping or that they
have low variance or a gaussian distribution.
3 Description of the Method
Figure 2 summarizes the three principal stages of the algorithm: (1) spikes
are detected automatically via amplitude thresholding; (2) the wavelet trans-

(A) The two-dimensional data points used as inputs. The different markers rep-

At temperature 0.05, the transition to the superparamagnetic phase occurs, and

form is calculated for each of the spikes and the optimal coefficients for
separating the spike classes are automatically selected; and (3) the selected
wavelet coefficients then serve as the input to the SPC algorithm, and cluster-
ing is performed after automatic selection of the temperature corresponding
to the superparamagnetic phase. (A Matlab implementation of the algorithm
can be obtained on-line from www.vis.caltech.edu/∼rodri.)
3.1 Spike Detection. Spike detection was performed by amplitude
thresholding after bandpass filtering the signal (300–6000 Hz, four pole

is used to cluster the spikes automatically.

Thr= 4σn; σn = median |x|

where x is the bandpass-filtered signal and σn is an estimate of the stan-
dard deviation of the background noise (Donoho & Johnstone, 1994). Note
that taking the standard deviation of the signal (including the spikes) could
lead to very high threshold values, especially in cases with high firing rates
and large spike amplitudes. In contrast, by using the estimation based on
the median, the interference of the spikes is diminished (under the reason-
able assumption that spikes amount to a small fraction of all samples). To
demonstrate this, we generated a segment of 10 sec of background noise
with unit standard deviation, and in successive simulations, we added a
distinct spike class with different firing rates. Figure 3 shows that for noise
alone (i.e., zero firing rate), both estimates are equal, but as the firing rate
increases, the standard deviation of the signal (conventional estimate) gives
an increasingly erroneous estimate of the noise level, whereas the improved
estimate from equation 3.1 remains close to the real value.
For each detected spike, 64 samples (i.e.,∼2.5 ms) were saved for further
analysis. All spikes were aligned to their maximum at data point 20. In
order to avoid spike misalignments due to low sampling, spike maxima
were determined from interpolated waveforms of 256 samples, using cubic
splines.
3.2 Selection of Wavelet Coefficients. After spikes are detected, their
wavelet transform is calculated, thus obtaining 64 wavelet coefficients for
each spike. We implemented a four-level multiresolution decomposition
using Haar wavelets. As explained in section 2.1, each wavelet coefficient
characterizes the spike shapes at different scales and times. The goal is to
select a few coefficients that best separate the different spike classes. Clearly,
such coefficients should have a multimodal distribution (unless there is
only one spike class). To perform this selection automatically, the Lilliefors
modification of a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test for normality was used
(Press, Teukolsky, Vetterling, & Flannery, 1992). Note that we do not rely on
any particular distribution of the data; rather, we are interested in deviation
from normality as a sign of a multimodal distribution. Given a data set x, the
test compares the cumulative distribution function of the data (F(x)) with
that of a gaussian distribution with the same mean and variance (G(x)).
Deviation from normality is then quantified by
max(|F(x)− G(x)|). (3.2)
In our implementation, the first 10 coefficients with the largest deviation
from normality were used. The selected set of wavelet coefficients provides

Overlapping spikes (i.e., spikes from different neurons appearing quasi-
simultaneously) introduce outliers in the distribution of the wavelet coeffi-
cients that cause deviations from normality in unimodal (as well as multi-
modal) distributions, thus compromising the use of the KS test as an estima-
tion of multimodality. In order to minimize this effect, for each coefficient
we only considered values within ±3 standard deviations.
3.3 SPC and Localization of the Superparamagnetic Phase. Once the
selected set of wavelet coefficients is chosen, we run the SPC algorithm for
a wide range of temperatures spanning the ferromagnetic, superparamag-
=== PAGE 10 ===
1670 R. Quiroga, Z. Nadasdy, and Y. Ben-Shaul
netic, and paramagnetic phases. In order to localize the superparamagnetic
phase automatically, a criterion based on the cluster sizes is used. The idea
is that for both the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases, temperature in-
creases can only lead to the creation of clusters with few members each. In-
deed, in the paramagnetic phase (i.e., high temperature), the clusters break
down into several small ones, and in the ferromagnetic phase, there are
almost no changes when the temperature is increased. In contrast, in the
superparamagnetic phase, increasing the temperature creates new clusters
with a large number of members.
In our implementation, we varied the temperature from 0 to 0.2 in in-
crements of 0.01 and looked for the highest temperature at which a clus-
ter containing more than 60 points appeared (not being present at lower
temperatures). Since our simulations were 60 sec long, this means that we
considered clusters corresponding to neurons with a mean firing rate of at
least 1 Hz. The threshold of 1 Hz gave us optimal results for all our sim-
ulations, but it should be decreased if one considers neurons with lower
firing rates. Alternatively, one can consider a fraction of the total number
of spikes. If no cluster with a minimum of 60 points was found, we kept
the minimum temperature value. Using this criterion, we can automatically
select the optimal temperature for cluster assignments, and therefore the
whole clustering procedure becomes unsupervised.
4 Data Simulation
Simulated signals were constructed using a database of 594 different av-
erage spike shapes compiled from recordings in the neocortex and basal
ganglia. For generating background noise, spikes randomly selected from
the database were superimposed at random times and amplitudes. This was
done for half the times of the samples. The rationale was to mimic the back-
ground noise of actual recordings that is generated by the activity of distant
neurons. Next, we superimposed a train of three distinct spike shapes (also
preselected from the same database of spikes) on the noise signal at random
times. The amplitude of the three spike classes was normalized to have a
peak value of 1. The noise level was determined from its standard deviation,
which was equal to 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2 relative to the amplitude of the
spike classes. In one case, since clustering was relatively easy, we also con-
sidered noise levels 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, and 0.4. Spike times and identities were
saved for subsequent evaluation of the clustering algorithm. The data were
first simulated at a sampling rate of 96,000 Hz, and by using interpolated
waveforms of the original spike shapes, we simulated the spike times to
fall continuously between samples (to machine precision). Finally, the data
were downsampled to 24,000 Hz. This procedure was introduced in order
to imitate actual recording conditions in which samples do not necessarily
fall on the same features within a spike (i.e., the peak of the signal does not
necessarily coincide with a discrete sample).

In all simulations, the three distinct spikes had a Poisson distribution
of interspike intervals with a mean firing rate of 20 Hz. A 2 ms refractory
period between spikes of the same class was introduced. Note that the back-
ground noise reproduces spike shape variability in biological signals (Fee,
Mitra, & Kleinfeld, 1996; Pouzat, Mazor, & Laurent, 2002). Moreover, con-
structing noise from spikes ensures that this noise shares a similar power
spectrum with the spikes themselves (1/f spectrum). The realistic simula-
tion conditions applied here render the entire procedure of spike sorting
more challenging than, for example, assuming a white noise distribution of
background activity. Further complications of real recordings (e.g., overlap-
ping spikes, bursting activity, moving electrodes) will be addressed in the
next section.
