5.4 Comparison with Other Spike Features. Errors of spike identifi-
cation cumulatively derive from two sources: incorrect feature extraction
and incorrect clustering. First, we compared the discrimination power of
wavelets at different noise levels with other feature extraction methods us-
ing the same clustering algorithm, SPC. Specifically, we compared the out-
come of classification with wavelets, principal component analysis (using
the first three principal components), the whole spike shape, and a fixed set
of spike features. The spike features were the mean square value of the sig-
nal (energy), the amplitude of the main peak, and the amplitude of the peaks
preceding and following it. The width of the spike (given by the position of
the three peaks) was also tested but found to worsen the spike classification.
Table 2 summarizes the results (examples 1 and 2 were shown in Figures 4
and 5, respectively). Performance was quantified in terms of the number of
classification errors and the number of clusters detected. Values in brackets
denote the number of clusters detected, when different from 3. Errors due
to overlapping spikes are not included in the table (but overlapping spikes
were also inputs to the algorithm). Since example 1 was easier to cluster, in
this case we also analyzed four higher noise levels.
In general, the best performance was achieved using the selected wavelet
coefficients as spike features. In fact, with wavelets, all three clusters are
correctly detected, with the exception of example 4, noise level 0.2. Using
the other features, only one cluster is detected when increasing the noise
level. Considering all wavelet coefficients as inputs to SPC (i.e., without the
selection based on the KS test) gave nearly the same results as those ob-
tained using the entire spike shape (not shown). This is not surprising since
the wavelet transform is linear, which implies rotations or rescaling of the
original high-dimensional space. The clear benefit is introduced when con-
sidering only those coefficients that allow a good separation between the
clusters, using the KS test. Note that PCA features gave slightly worse re-
sults than those using the entire spike shapes (and clearly worse than using
wavelets). Therefore, PCA gives a reasonable solution when using clustering
algorithms that cannot handle high-dimensional spaces (although this is not
a problem for SPC). The fixed features, such as peak amplitudes and mean
squared values, were much less efficient. This was expected since spike
classes were generated with the same peak value and in some cases also
with very similar shapes that could not be discriminated by these features.
We remark that the number of detected clusters decreases monotonically
with noise level, but the number of classification errors does not necessarily
increase monotonically because even when three clusters are correctly rec-
ognized, a large number of spikes may remain unassigned to any of them
(see, e.g., example 4 with PCA for noise levels 0.05 and 0.1).

ferent clustering algorithms can be applied for spike sorting, and the choice
of an optimal one is important in order to exploit the discrimination power

when spike shapes are more similar (Table 2, examples 3 and 4). We remark

to the presence of more elongated cluster shapes obtained with wavelets

6 Discussion
We presented a method for detection and sorting neuronal multiunit activ-
ity. The procedure is fully unsupervised and fast, thus being particularly
interesting for the classification of spikes from a large number of channels
recorded simultaneously. To obtain a quantitative measure of its perfor-
mance, the method was tested on simulated data sets with different noise
levels and similar spike shapes. The noise was generated by superposition of
a large number of small-amplitude spikes, resembling characteristics of real
recordings. This makes the spectral characteristics of noise and spikes simi-
lar, thus increasing the difficulty in detection and clustering. The proposed
method had an overall better performance than conventional approaches,
such as using PCA for extracting spike features or K-means for clustering.
Spike detection was achieved by using an amplitude threshold on the
high-pass filtered data. The threshold value was calculated automatically
using the median of the absolute value of the signal. The advantage of this
estimation, rather than using the variance of the overall signal, is that it
diminishes the dependence of the threshold on the firing rate and the peak-
to-peak amplitude of the spikes, thus giving an improved estimation of the
background noise level. Indeed, high firing rates and high spike amplitudes
lead to an overestimation of the appropriate threshold value. In terms of the
number of misses and number of false positives, the proposed automatic
detection procedure had good performance for the different examples and
noise levels.
The advantage of using the wavelet transform as a feature extractor is that
very localized shape differences of the different units can be discerned. The
information about the shape of the spikes is distributed in several wavelet
coefficients, whereas with PCA, most of the information about the spike
shapes is captured only by the first three principal components (Letelier
& Weber, 2000; Hulata, Segev, Shapira, Benveniste, & Ben-Jacob, 2000; Hu-
lata, Segev, & Ben-Jacob, 2002), which are not necessarily optimal for cluster
identification (see Figure 7). Moreover, wavelet coefficients are localized
in time. In agreement with these considerations, a better performance of

wavelet coefficients in comparison with PCA was shown for several exam-
ples generated with different noise levels. For comparison, we also used the
whole spike shape as input to the clustering algorithm. As shown in Table
2, the dimensionality reduction achieved with the KS test clearly improves
the clustering performance. Since wavelets are a linear transform, using all
the wavelet coefficients yields nearly the same results as taking the entire
spike shape (as it is just a rescaling of the space). Since the need of a low-
dimensional space is a limiting factor for many clustering algorithms, the
dimensionality reduction achieved by combining wavelets with the KS test
may have a broad range of interest.
The use of wavelets for spike sorting has been proposed recently by Lete-
lier et al. (2000) and Hulata et al. (2000, 2002). Our approach differs from
theirs in several aspects, most notably by the implementation of our algo-
rithm as a single unsupervised process. One key feature of our algorithm
is the choice of wavelet coefficients by using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of
normality, thus selecting features that give an optimal separation between
the different clusters. Letelier et al. (2000) suggested to visually select those
wavelet coefficients with the largest mean, variance, and, most fundamen-
tal, multimodal distribution. However, neither a large average nor a large
variance entitles the given coefficient to be the best separator. In contrast, we
considered only the multimodality of the distributions. In this respect, we
showed that coefficients in the low-frequency bands, with a large variance
and uniform distribution, are not appropriate for the separation of distinct
clusters. In contrast, they introduce dimensions with nonsegregated distri-
butions that in practice may compromise the performance of the clustering
algorithm. A caveat of the KS test as an estimator of multimodality is that it
can also select unimodal nongaussian distributions (those that are skewed
or have large kurtosis). In fact, this was the case of three coefficients shown
in Figure 7. Despite this limitation, the selection of wavelet coefficients with
the KS test gave optimal results that indeed outperformed other feature
selection methods.

variance of the data are selected, but these directions do not necessarily pro-
vide the best separation of the spike classes. In other words, it may well be
that the information for separating the clusters is represented in principal
components with low eigenvalues, which are usually disregarded. In this
respect, our method is more reminiscent of independent component anal-
ysis (ICA), where directions with a minimum of mutual information are
chosen. Moreover, it has been shown that minimum mutual information
is related to maximum deviation from normality (Hyvarinen & Oja, 2000).
Hulata et al. (2000, 2002) proposed a criterion based on the mutual informa-
tion of all pairs of cluster combinations for selecting the best wavelet packet
coefficients. However, such an approach cannot be implemented in an un-
supervised way. In fact, Hulata and coworkers used previous knowledge
of the spike classes for selecting the best wavelet packets. A second caveat

is the difficulty of estimating mutual information (Quian Quiroga, Kraskov,
Kreuz, & Grassberger, 2002) in comparison with the KS test of normality.

perparamagnetic clustering. This method is based on K-nearest neighbor
interactions and therefore does not require low variance, nonoverlapping
clusters, or a priori assumptions of a certain distribution of the data (e.g.,
gaussian). Superparamagnetic clustering has already been applied with ex-
cellent results to several clustering problems (Blatt et al., 1996, 1997; Do-
many, 1999). In our study, we demonstrated for the first time its applica-
tion to spike sorting. Moreover, it is possible to automatically locate the
superparamagnetic regime, thus making the entire sorting procedure un-
supervised. Besides the obvious advantage of unsupervised clustering, we
compared the results obtained with SPC to those obtained using K-means
(with Euclidean distance). Although this comparison should not be gen-

of SPC over methods that rely on the presence of gaussian distributions,
clusters with centers inside the cluster (see Figure 1 for counterexamples),

content.text:
# Summary: Quiroga, Nadasdy & Ben-Shaul (2004)

**The problem.** Sorting spikes by hand is slow and biased. Automatic methods usually rely on features like PCA and on clustering methods that assume Gaussian clusters, and both assumptions can fail. The authors build a pipeline that runs with no human input and test it on simulated data, where the correct answers are known. That is the same strategy as your project.

**The pipeline:**
1. **Detection.**
   - They bandpass filter at **300–6000 Hz** with a 4-pole Butterworth filter.
   - The threshold is 4σₙ, with σₙ = median(|x|)/0.6745. Their Fig. 3 is your "robust σ vs. plain std" check: as firing rate rises, plain std overestimates the noise, while the median estimate stays close to the true value.
   - They save **64 samples** per spike (about 2.5 ms) and align each spike so its peak sits at sample 20. The peak is found on a cubic-spline upsampled version of the waveform.
2. **Features.**
   - They apply a 4-level Haar transform, which gives 64 coefficients per spike.
   - They keep the **10 coefficients** whose distributions are least normal, measured with the Lilliefors version of the KS test.
   - The reasoning: a coefficient that separates neurons should have several peaks in its distribution, and a distribution with several peaks isn't Gaussian.
   - Before testing, they keep only values within ±3 SD, so overlapping spikes don't make a coefficient look non-normal.
   - In their Fig. 7, picking coefficients by highest variance instead gives flat, single-peaked distributions that don't separate anything.
3. **Clustering: superparamagnetic clustering (SPC).**
   - Each spike's neighbors in feature space tend to change state together at a given "temperature."
   - At low temperature everything forms one cluster. At high temperature it breaks into dust. In between, the real clusters appear.
   - They choose the temperature automatically: the highest one at which a new cluster with more than 60 spikes appears.
   - SPC makes no Gaussian assumption.

**How they simulated data.**
- Spike shapes come from a database of 594 *real* recorded spikes, with each peak scaled to 1.
- **Background noise is made of many randomly placed small spikes from that database.** That gives the noise the same spectrum as the spikes, which makes sorting harder than white noise would.
- Three neurons fire as Poisson processes at 20 Hz with a 2 ms refractory period.
- Noise SD is 0.05–0.2 of the spike peak (up to 0.4 in one example).
- They simulate at 96 kHz and then downsample to 24 kHz, so spike peaks don't line up exactly with samples.

**Results:**
- **Detection (Table 1):** they miss few spikes until noise reaches 0.2.
  - One neuron had a positive-first spike, and the positive-only threshold missed many of its spikes.
  - When noise is very low, a spike's second peak can cross threshold and get counted as a second spike (a false positive).
- **Sorting (Table 2):**
  - With SPC, the average error count was 232 for wavelets, 1092 for PCA, and 873 for the raw waveform.
  - **With K-means, the gap almost disappeared: 332 vs. 371.** In a few cases PCA did better, because wavelet clusters were stretched out in a way K-means can't handle.
  - The number of clusters found drops as noise rises.
- **Harder conditions:** SPC + wavelets still found all three neurons in three tests: an electrode drifting (amplitude falling from 1 to 0.3), a bursting neuron (spike amplitudes 1.0, 0.7, 0.5 about 3 ms apart), and spike amplitude tied to the background signal.
- Most errors came from overlapping spikes less than about 0.5 ms apart.

## Where your plan differs from the paper (I recommend recording these)
1. **Filter band:** your plan uses 300–3000 Hz; the paper uses 300–6000 Hz. That's fine, but you'll need to justify the choice on Dec 3. It also changes your Rice's-formula prediction, because f_rms depends on the band.
2. **Spike polarity:** the paper detects positive peaks only. Your HH extracellular spikes will be **negative first**, so your detector needs a negative threshold or |x|. This is a real design decision, not just a detail.
3. **GMM vs. SPC:** this was already recorded. The K-means result matters for you, though: GMM shares K-means' Gaussian assumption, so your wavelet advantage may be small. If your "wavelets match or beat PCA" check comes out narrow, this is the likely reason, and it's a finding, not a bug.
4. **Waveforms and noise:** the paper uses real recorded spike shapes and builds noise from spikes. You use HH waveforms. Your plan for realistic background noise matches the paper's approach.

The paper also gives you ready-made test parameters for later, for example the bursting neuron (1.0/0.7/0.5, about 3 ms apart) and the noise levels 0.05–0.2.

## Check your understanding: paper questions
1. Why does selecting coefficients by *non-normality* find better features than selecting by *variance*? Refer to the paper's Fig. 7 idea.
2. Why might wavelets beat PCA by a lot with SPC but only slightly with K-means? What does that predict for your GMM?
3. Their noise is made from real spikes rather than white noise. Why does that make sorting harder?

Your three HH quiz questions from earlier (the refractory period, the 50 → 100 µm numbers, and Euler with a step that's too large) are still open. We'll finish those before writing the HH integrator.

**Still to do for Week 0:** make the first commit with your own message and create the GitHub repo.

## Differences from Quiroga et al. (2004)

This project starts from Quian Quiroga, Nadasdy & Ben-Shaul (2004) but departs from it in four places. Each is listed with what the paper did, what this project does, why, and what it changes when comparing results.

### 1. Filter band

- **Paper:** bandpass 300–6000 Hz.
- **This project:** 300–6000 Hz by default, matching the paper, with the band exposed as a parameter.
- **Why:** matching the paper keeps detection results comparable. Making the band adjustable lets the app show the trade-off directly: a narrower band admits less noise but removes the sharp, fast features that help tell similar neurons apart.
- **What it changes:** the false-detection prediction depends on the band. Rice's formula uses the RMS frequency f_rms of the filtered noise, which is computed from the actual filter's frequency response. For an ideal 300–6000 Hz band, f_rms ≈ 3.6 kHz; for 300–3000 Hz, f_rms ≈ 1.8 kHz. The sampling rate must sit well above twice the upper cutoff.

### 2. Spike polarity

- **Paper:** detects positive peaks only.
- **This project:** detects negative peaks only, with threshold x < −4σ, where σ = median(|x|) / 0.6745.
- **Why:** extracellular spikes derived from a Hodgkin–Huxley action potential are negative first. A negative-only threshold is the exact mirror of the paper's one-sided detection, keeps false positives low, and lets spikes align on their trough.
- **What it changes:** because only one tail counts, the expected false-positive numbers are one-sided:
  - per-sample probability of a noise sample below −4σ: 1 − Φ(4) ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵;
  - false detections per second on filtered noise (Rice's formula): ≈ f_rms × exp(−8), about 1.2 per second for an ideal 300–6000 Hz band.

### 3. Clustering method

- **Paper:** superparamagnetic clustering (SPC), a method from statistical physics that does not assume Gaussian clusters and chooses the number of clusters itself.
- **This project:** a Gaussian mixture model fitted by expectation–maximization (EM), with the number of neurons chosen by BIC.
- **Why:** EM can be checked rigorously (the likelihood must never decrease, and it recovers known parameters on synthetic mixtures), can be written and explained from scratch within one semester, and runs fast enough for an interactive web app.
- **What it changes:** like K-means, a GMM favors compact, roughly Gaussian clusters. The paper found a smaller wavelet advantage when clustering with K-means than with SPC, so the right published reference for this project is the paper's K-means comparison. If wavelet features beat PCA by only a narrow margin here, that is an expected consequence of the clustering method, not a bug.

### 4. Spike waveforms and noise

- **Paper:** spike shapes taken from real recordings; background noise built from spikes.
- **This project:** spike shapes derived from a Hodgkin–Huxley simulation; background noise built from the summed spikes of many distant neurons, following the paper's approach.
- **Why:** simulating the waveform from biophysics makes every step of the recording model explainable and adjustable, with no external data.
- **What it changes:**
  - Hodgkin–Huxley's original parameters come from the squid giant axon and produce slower spikes than typical mammalian cortical spikes (about 1 ms). Spike width is measured, and a temperature correction to the rate constants is applied if needed. Width also determines how much of each spike survives the filter band.
  - Neurons that share one waveform scaled by distance differ only in amplitude. To vary shape, waveforms come from a small precomputed library built from several Hodgkin–Huxley parameter sets, with distance-dependent smoothing (far neurons lose their sharpest features).
  - Results describe sorting performance on these simulated waveforms; real spike shapes may be more or less separable.

I copied your file into the project unchanged, as [README_deviations.md](README_deviations.md), and checked it. It's good: each deviation says what the paper did, what you do, why, and what it changes.

## The numbers check out
| Claim | Recomputed |
| --- | --- |
| f_rms, ideal 300–6000 Hz | 3554 Hz ≈ 3.6 kHz ✓ |
| f_rms, ideal 300–3000 Hz | 1825 Hz ≈ 1.8 kHz ✓ |
| 1 − Φ(4) | 3.17 × 10⁻⁵ ✓ |
| One-sided Rice estimate, 300–6000 Hz | 1.19 /s ✓ |

The old CLAUDE.md prediction (both sides, 300–3000 Hz) was 1.22 /s, so the two setups land at almost the same false-detection rate by coincidence. The wider band doubles f_rms, and dropping the positive side halves the count. That would make a nice point on Dec 3.

## Three things to tighten
1. **Section 3 overstates the comparison with K-means.** A GMM with full covariance matrices *can* fit long, tilted ellipses, which is exactly the cluster shape the paper says K-means failed on. What a GMM can't fit is *curved* or lopsided clusters, like the stretched cluster a bursting neuron would make. So the K-means comparison is a lower bound on how well you might do, not a match. I'd change "like K-means, a GMM favors compact clusters" to say that.
2. **Section 1, computing f_rms:** if your filter is zero-phase (running the filter forward and then backward), its effective magnitude response is |H|², not |H|. Compute f_rms from |H|² or your Rice estimate will be off. A real 4-pole Butterworth also lets through more high frequencies than an ideal band does, so expect a measured f_rms a bit above 3.6 kHz. Also, "well above twice the upper cutoff" should name an actual sampling rate. The paper uses 24 kHz.
3. **Section 4 has two open points:**
   - **"Temperature correction if needed."** Choose the criterion now, for example: rescale the rate constants until the trough-to-peak width is about 1 ms. Write down the formula you'll use (the Q10 factor 3^((T − 6.3)/10)).
   - **Distance-dependent smoothing** is a modeling assumption, not something HH gives you. On Dec 3 you'll need a physical reason for it, or else label it clearly as an assumption.

**One related risk:** negative-only detection is safe only if *every* waveform in your library is negative first. The paper's biggest miss rate came from exactly this problem with the opposite sign. Make it a test: for each library waveform, check that its largest-magnitude peak is negative.

## Where CLAUDE.md now disagrees with this file
- The pipeline still says 300–3000 Hz and ~4σ in both directions.
- The detection checks are still the two-sided numbers: 6.3 × 10⁻⁵ and the two-sided Rice formula. (The exceedance-fraction check can stay two-sided as a pure statistics test, if you like.)
- The Dec 3 prep list still says "why 300–3000 Hz."
- Your new scope isn't on the roadmap yet: the waveform library, the temperature correction and the adjustable filter band. Each one costs time in an already tight Week 1–2.

**Still open:** the Week 0 commit and the GitHub repo, the three paper questions, and the three HH quiz questions.

# Spike sorting project — context for Claude Code

This is my final project for 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026). I work on it alone, with you as collaborator. The course grades whether I *learn* the science and the computation, not just whether the code works. Read the "How to work with me" section before doing anything.

## The project in one paragraph

I simulate extracellular brain recordings where the true spike times are known, then sort them with a spike sorter I write myself, to measure how many neurons a single electrode can reliably tell apart. The final product is an interactive web app.

**Scientific question:** How many distinct neurons can be reliably separated from a single electrode's signal, and how do noise level, waveform similarity and firing rate limit that number?

**Inspiring paper:** Quian Quiroga, Nadasdy & Ben-Shaul (2004), *Unsupervised spike detection and sorting with wavelets and superparamagnetic clustering*, Neural Computation (PDF in `papers/`).
**Related:** Pedreira et al. (2012), *How many neurons can we see with current spike sorting algorithms?*; Trautmann et al. (2019), sorting vs. unsorted threshold crossings (optional extension).
**Data:** none — everything is simulated, so ground truth is exact.

## Pipeline

1. **Simulator**
   - Spike trains: Poisson firing with a refractory period (~2 ms).
   - Waveforms: one Hodgkin–Huxley action potential (my own ODE integrator, e.g. RK4), converted to an extracellular waveform (tracks membrane current, not voltage), scaled by each neuron's distance from the electrode.
   - Recording: waveforms placed at spike times, summed, plus background noise (aim for realistic background from many distant neurons, not only white noise).
   - Output: voltage trace + answer key of true spike times and identities.
2. **Sorter (all core steps written by me, from scratch)**
   - Bandpass filter, zero-phase; band is a parameter, default 300–6000 Hz (matches the paper).
   - Negative-only threshold detection: x < −4σ, with robust noise estimate σ = median(|x|) / 0.6745, plus a dead time after each detection.
   - Align detected spikes on their trough.
   - Multilevel Haar wavelet transform; select coefficients by deviation from normality (KS test).
   - PCA features as a baseline for comparison.
   - Gaussian mixture model fitted by EM; number of neurons chosen by BIC (lowest BIC wins).
   - Scoring: match sorted spikes to true spikes within a fixed time window.
3. **Web app:** sliders for number of neurons, noise, waveform similarity, firing rate; panels for raw trace with sorted spikes, feature space, cluster waveforms, accuracy vs. ground truth; a sweep view of neurons recovered vs. neurons present.

## Differences from Quiroga et al. (2004)

Full write-up (paper vs. us, why, what it changes) lives in the README. Don't drift back to the paper's method on these:

1. **Filter band:** default 300–6000 Hz like the paper, but exposed as a parameter. f_rms (and so Rice's prediction) depends on the band.
2. **Polarity:** paper detects positive peaks; HH extracellular spikes are negative first, so we use a negative-only threshold (one-sided, mirror of the paper).
3. **Clustering:** GMM + EM with BIC instead of superparamagnetic clustering. GMM shares K-means' preference for compact Gaussian clusters, so compare against the paper's K-means result; a narrow wavelet advantage is a finding, not a bug.
4. **Waveforms:** HH-derived instead of real recorded shapes (check spike width ~1 ms; apply temperature correction if too slow). Shape variety via a small precomputed library of HH parameter sets plus distance-dependent smoothing (planned Week 5; Week 4 uses amplitude-only differences). Background noise from many distant neurons' spikes, like the paper.

## Other decisions

- **Libraries only for plumbing** (arrays, plotting, possibly the filter design). The course rejects "one library call fed into the next." Detection, Haar transform, coefficient selection, EM, BIC and scoring are mine.
- **Detection false-positive checks (one-sided, corrected Oct 30).** 1 − Φ(4) ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ is a *per-sample* probability. After filtering, neighboring samples are correlated, so one noise bump spans several samples but counts as one detection. Therefore:
  - Fraction of noise *samples* below −4σ should match 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ (white or filtered, with σ measured after filtering).
  - Detections per sample should match 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ only on **white** noise.
  - On **filtered** noise, detections per second should match Rice's formula for one-sided crossings: ≈ f_rms × exp(−u²/2) at u = 4, with f_rms computed from my filter's actual frequency response (ideal 300–6000 Hz band: f_rms ≈ 3.6 kHz → ≈ 1.2 false detections/s). Approximate because the signal is sampled.
- **Possible GMM stress test:** a bursting neuron (shrinking amplitude stretches its cluster) to see whether GMM wrongly splits it.

## Checks the project must pass

- Ground truth scoring: detection rate, false positives, assignment accuracy.
- Detection-rate checks above (one-sided exceedance fraction, white-noise detections, Rice's formula on filtered noise).
- Spike width of the HH-derived extracellular waveform is close to ~1 ms.
- Robust σ recovers true σ on pure noise and stays accurate as firing rate rises, while plain std overestimates.
- Two very different neurons, no noise → perfect sorting.
- Haar transform inverts exactly; hand-computed 8-sample example matches code.
- EM recovers known parameters of a synthetic Gaussian mixture; log-likelihood rises every iteration.
- Published behavior: wavelets match or beat PCA as sorting gets harder, compared against the paper's K-means result (Quiroga 2004); neurons recovered level off as more are added (Pedreira 2012).
- Refractory violations (<2 ms intervals) near zero for correct units, high for merged ones.
- With a fixed random seed, the app reproduces offline script results.

## Roadmap and course deadlines

Full week-by-week plan with action items: see `ROADMAP.md`.

| Week | Dates | Phase | Course deadline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Oct 8–14 | Simulate one neuron (HH, waveform, spike trains) | Proposal feedback Oct 9 |
| 2 | Oct 15–21 | Full recording, filtering, detection | Journal checkpoint 1 — Oct 21 |
| 3 | Oct 22–30 | Alignment, Haar features, PCA baseline | Journal checkpoint 2 — Oct 30 |
| 4 | Oct 31–Nov 6 | EM-GMM, BIC, scoring, first end-to-end sort | TA check-ins open Nov 4 |
| 5 | Nov 7–13 | Parameter sweeps; answer the question | TA check-in by Nov 13 |
| 6 | Nov 14–20 | Web app v1, deployed; README draft | App live + checkpoint 3 — Nov 20 |
| 7 | Nov 21–27 | Fixes; optional sorted-vs-unsorted extension | Thanksgiving Break |
| 8 | Nov 28–Dec 1 | README, ≤5-min video, demo prep | Final app/code/video + demo day — Dec 1 |
| — | Dec 3 | — | Closed, on-paper project assessment |

**Current status:** _(update me)_

## How to work with me

My session logs are graded as a build journal. The graders look for learning, steady work, and checking — so:

- **Teach before building.** When we start a new concept (filtering, wavelets, EM, Rice's formula…), explain it first, then quiz me and let me explain it back before writing code.
- **Explain code you write.** After writing anything non-trivial, walk me through what it does and why. Expect me to ask "why?" often.
- **Debug with me, don't just fix.** When something breaks, help me form hypotheses and test them rather than silently patching it.
- **Always tie work to a check.** New code should come with a test or a comparison against one of the checks above.
- **Keep scope small.** Get the smallest version working and checked before adding features.
- **Don't write my commit messages** — remind me to write them in my own words.
- **Flag deviations.** If something we do departs from the paper or this file, say so and suggest recording it (README or here).
- **Prepare me for Dec 3.** I must be able to explain, without notes: the extracellular spike shape and distance scaling; HH variables and my integrator; why 300–6000 Hz and what changing the band does; where 0.6745 comes from; why a negative-only threshold; the one-sided 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ derivation, why filtered noise gives fewer detections, and Rice's prediction; each of the four differences from Quiroga et al. and what it costs; a Haar transform by hand; why non-Gaussian coefficients are chosen; EM steps, monotone likelihood, and what BIC trades off; scoring and refractory violations; my answer with its numbers; and what the simulation leaves out.

content.text:
These are all solid now. Notes on each:

**1. Correct, and in your own words.** You have the right mechanism: the positive feedback loop (depolarization opens m → Na⁺ flows in → more depolarization). You also split it correctly into the absolute refractory period (h closed, so the loop can't start at any stimulus strength) and the relative one (h recovering and n still open, so the stimulus has to be stronger). That would earn full marks on Dec 3.

**2. Correct: ½ and ¼, and the conclusion is right.** Here's one step further, for later: the electrode detects every neuron within some radius R, and the number of neurons in that region grows like R³.
- Under 1/r, doubling the noise halves R, which leaves **8× fewer** detectable neurons.
- Under 1/r², R only shrinks by √2, which leaves about **2.8× fewer**.

So the law you choose changes how your answer depends on noise, not just the raw count. You still need to pick a law, but not until we build the waveform. It doesn't affect the integrator.

**3. Right idea. Here's the number:** 400 mV/ms × 0.5 ms = **200 mV in one step**, from about −55 to about +145 mV, far past E_Na (+50).

The key physics: above E_Na, the driving force (V − E_Na) changes sign, so the "sodium current" now pushes V *down*, hard. The next step overshoots the other way, and the trace oscillates or blows up. The gate updates can also push m, h and n outside [0, 1], which is physically impossible.

RK4 isn't immune to this either. That's why we'll use dt ≈ 0.01 ms and *check* it, not assume it.

## Next: the HH integrator
These are the checks it will need to pass:
- With no input, V settles at about −65 mV.
- A brief current pulse gives exactly one spike, which peaks below E_Na.
- m, h and n always stay within [0, 1].
- **Convergence:** halving dt barely changes the spike.
- **Order of accuracy:** halving dt cuts RK4's error about 16× and Euler's about 2×. That's your Q4 answer turned into a test.

Before I set anything up, I need two decisions from you:

1. **Language:** Python, or something else your course uses (for example Go)? This also affects how we build the web app later.
2. **Who writes what:** CLAUDE.md calls the integrator "my own." I suggest **you write the RK4 step and the HH right-hand side**, and I set up the project skeleton and the tests listed above, then review your code with you. Or would you rather I write a first version and walk you through it line by line?

"""Hodgkin-Huxley model of one patch of membrane, with hand-written integrators.

Units: time in ms, voltage in mV, current density in uA/cm^2,
conductance in mS/cm^2, capacitance in uF/cm^2.

The state is a length-4 array y = [V, m, h, n].
"""

import math

import numpy as np

# Classic HH parameters (squid axon, 6.3 C), shifted so rest is near -65 mV.
C_M = 1.0       # membrane capacitance
G_NA = 120.0    # max sodium conductance
G_K = 36.0      # max potassium conductance
G_L = 0.3       # leak conductance
E_NA = 50.0     # sodium reversal potential
E_K = -77.0     # potassium reversal potential
E_L = -54.387   # leak reversal, chosen so the resting potential is -65 mV
V_REST = -65.0


def _x_over_1_minus_exp(x, k):
    """Return x / (1 - exp(-x / k)), using its limit k when x is near 0.

    alpha_m and alpha_n have this form; plugging in x = 0 directly would
    divide 0 by 0.
    """
    if abs(x) < 1e-6:
        return k
    return x / (1.0 - math.exp(-x / k))


def rates(v):
    """Opening (alpha) and closing (beta) rates of the m, h, n gates at voltage v, in 1/ms."""
    alpha_m = 0.1 * _x_over_1_minus_exp(v + 40.0, 10.0)
    beta_m = 4.0 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 18.0)
    alpha_h = 0.07 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 20.0)
    beta_h = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-(v + 35.0) / 10.0))
    alpha_n = 0.01 * _x_over_1_minus_exp(v + 55.0, 10.0)
    beta_n = 0.125 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 80.0)
    return alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n


def steady_state(v):
    """State [v, m, h, n] with every gate at its equilibrium value for a fixed v."""
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = rates(v)
    m = alpha_m / (alpha_m + beta_m)
    h = alpha_h / (alpha_h + beta_h)
    n = alpha_n / (alpha_n + beta_n)
    return np.array([v, m, h, n])


def ionic_currents(y):
    """Sodium, potassium and leak currents (outward positive) for state y."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na = G_NA * m**3 * h * (v - E_NA)
    i_k = G_K * n**4 * (v - E_K)
    i_l = G_L * (v - E_L)
    return i_na, i_k, i_l


def hh_rhs(t, y, i_ext):
    """dy/dt for the HH equations; i_ext is a function of time giving injected current."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na, i_k, i_l = ionic_currents(y)
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = rates(v)

    dv = (i_ext(t) - i_na - i_k - i_l) / C_M
    dm = alpha_m * (1.0 - m) - beta_m * m
    dh = alpha_h * (1.0 - h) - beta_h * h
    dn = alpha_n * (1.0 - n) - beta_n * n
    return np.array([dv, dm, dh, dn])


def euler_step(f, t, y, dt):
    """One forward-Euler step: follow the slope at the start for the whole step."""
    return y + dt * f(t, y)


def rk4_step(f, t, y, dt):
    """One classical Runge-Kutta (RK4) step: a weighted average of four slopes."""
    k1 = f(t, y)
    k2 = f(t + dt / 2, y + dt / 2 * k1)
    k3 = f(t + dt / 2, y + dt / 2 * k2)
    k4 = f(t + dt, y + dt * k3)
    return y + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)


def no_current(t):
    return 0.0


def pulse(start, duration, amplitude):
    """Current that is `amplitude` for start <= t < start + duration, else 0."""
    def i_ext(t):
        return amplitude if start <= t < start + duration else 0.0
    return i_ext


def simulate(t_max, dt, i_ext=no_current, y0=None, method="rk4"):
    """Integrate the HH equations from t = 0 to t_max.

    Returns (t, y): t has shape (n_steps + 1,), y has shape (n_steps + 1, 4)
    with columns V, m, h, n. Starts at rest unless y0 is given.
    """
    step = {"rk4": rk4_step, "euler": euler_step}[method]
    n_steps = int(round(t_max / dt))
    t = np.arange(n_steps + 1) * dt
    y = np.empty((n_steps + 1, 4))
    y[0] = steady_state(V_REST) if y0 is None else y0

    def f(t_now, y_now):
        return hh_rhs(t_now, y_now, i_ext)

    for i in range(n_steps):
        y[i + 1] = step(f, t[i], y[i], dt)
    return t, y


def count_spikes(v, threshold=0.0):
    """Number of upward crossings of `threshold` mV in a voltage trace."""
    above = v >= threshold
    return int(np.sum(~above[:-1] & above[1:]))

"""Checks for the Hodgkin-Huxley integrator (CLAUDE.md, Week 1)."""

import numpy as np
import pytest

from spikesort import hh


def test_rest_stays_at_rest():
    # With no input, a cell started at rest should stay near -65 mV.
    t, y = hh.simulate(t_max=50.0, dt=0.01)
    assert np.max(np.abs(y[:, 0] - hh.V_REST)) < 0.5


def test_suprathreshold_pulse_gives_one_spike_below_e_na():
    t, y = hh.simulate(t_max=30.0, dt=0.01, i_ext=hh.pulse(5.0, 1.0, 10.0))
    v = y[:, 0]
    assert hh.count_spikes(v) == 1
    assert v.max() < hh.E_NA       # the peak can approach E_Na but never pass it
    assert v.max() > 20.0          # and it is a real spike, not a bump


def test_subthreshold_pulse_gives_no_spike():
    t, y = hh.simulate(t_max=30.0, dt=0.01, i_ext=hh.pulse(5.0, 1.0, 1.0))
    assert hh.count_spikes(y[:, 0]) == 0


def test_gates_stay_between_0_and_1():
    t, y = hh.simulate(t_max=30.0, dt=0.01, i_ext=hh.pulse(5.0, 1.0, 10.0))
    gates = y[:, 1:]
    assert gates.min() >= 0.0 and gates.max() <= 1.0


def test_halving_dt_barely_changes_the_spike():
    i_ext = hh.pulse(5.0, 1.0, 10.0)
    t1, y1 = hh.simulate(t_max=15.0, dt=0.01, i_ext=i_ext)
    t2, y2 = hh.simulate(t_max=15.0, dt=0.005, i_ext=i_ext)
    peak_time_1 = t1[np.argmax(y1[:, 0])]
    peak_time_2 = t2[np.argmax(y2[:, 0])]
    assert abs(peak_time_1 - peak_time_2) <= 0.01      # within one coarse step
    assert abs(y1[:, 0].max() - y2[:, 0].max()) < 0.1  # peak voltage within 0.1 mV


def _error_ratio(method, dt):
    """How much the error shrinks when dt is halved, estimated from runs at dt, dt/2, dt/4.

    The difference between the dt and dt/2 runs is about C*dt^p, and between
    dt/2 and dt/4 about C*(dt/2)^p, so their ratio is about 2^p. No exact
    solution is needed. The cell starts depolarized to -50 mV with no injected
    current, so the right-hand side is smooth and it fires one spike.
    """
    y0 = hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST)
    y0[0] = -50.0
    runs = [hh.simulate(t_max=10.0, dt=dt / 2**k, y0=y0, method=method)[1][:, 0]
            for k in range(3)]
    # Compare all three runs on the coarse run's time grid.
    v_dt, v_half, v_quarter = runs[0], runs[1][::2], runs[2][::4]
    return np.max(np.abs(v_dt - v_half)) / np.max(np.abs(v_half - v_quarter))


def test_rk4_is_fourth_order():
    # 2^4 = 16
    assert _error_ratio("rk4", 0.02) == pytest.approx(16, rel=0.25)


def test_euler_is_first_order():
    # 2^1 = 2
    assert _error_ratio("euler", 0.01) == pytest.approx(2, rel=0.25)

The HH integrator is written and all 7 checks pass (`.venv/bin/pytest -v`, 0.6 s). Here's what I added, the numbers it produced, and then the line-by-line walkthrough.

**Setup:**
- A Python virtual environment in `.venv/` with numpy and pytest. Versions are pinned in `requirements.txt`.
- [pytest.ini](pytest.ini), which tells pytest where the tests are and lets them import your code.
- The `spikesort/` package and the `tests/` folder.
- I also added `.pytest_cache/` to `.gitignore`.

## What the checks measured
| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Rest, no input, 50 ms | drifted at most **0.007 mV** from −65 |
| 10 µA/cm² pulse for 1 ms | **1 spike**, peak **+39.1 mV** (below E_Na = 50), dip to −76.2 mV, back to −64.8 mV |
| 1 µA/cm² pulse | 0 spikes (below threshold) |
| Gates | stayed within [0, 1] |
| dt 0.01 → 0.005 ms | peak time and peak height essentially unchanged |
| Euler error ratio | **1.98** (theory: 2) |
| RK4 error ratio | **19.1** at dt = 0.02 ms; **17.4** at 0.01 ms (theory: 16) |

**The RK4 ratio isn't exactly 16, and it's still correct.** "Error ∝ dt⁴" is only exactly true once dt is small enough. At dt = 0.04, 0.02 and 0.01 ms, the ratio went 23.5 → 19.1 → 17.4, getting closer to 16 each time. That trend is evidence the code really is 4th order. The test allows ±25%.

**Your Q4 answer, run for real:** with Euler at dt = 0.1, 0.2 or 0.5 ms, the simulation blew up. At 0.5 ms, V reached +18,000 mV, the gates left [0, 1], and the values ended as NaN. RK4 at 0.01 ms stays well behaved.

## Walkthrough of [hh.py](spikesort/hh.py)

**Lines 1–22: units and parameters.** These are the classic HH values. E_L = −54.387 is chosen so that the leak current exactly cancels the small Na and K currents at −65 mV. That's what makes −65 mV the resting potential. *This is the squid axon at 6.3 °C with no temperature correction yet*, as your deviation #4 says. The ~1 ms width check belongs to the waveform step, which comes next.

**Lines 25–34: `_x_over_1_minus_exp`.** α_m and α_n have the form x / (1 − e^(−x/k)). At V = −40 mV (for m) or −55 mV (for n), x = 0 and this becomes 0/0. Mathematically the limit is k, so the function returns k when x is essentially 0. Without this, a trace that passed exactly through −40.000 mV would crash.

**Lines 37–45: `rates(v)`.** These are the six standard HH rate functions in 1/ms. α is how fast closed gates open and β is how fast open gates close. Notice that α_m grows steeply with depolarization, which is the start of your positive feedback loop. α_h *falls* with depolarization while β_h rises, so h closes.

**Lines 48–54: `steady_state(v)`.** If V were held fixed, each gate would settle where opening balances closing: α(1 − x) = βx, so x∞ = α / (α + β). We start the simulation from these values at −65 mV, so the cell begins truly at rest. That's why the rest test drifts only 0.007 mV.

**Lines 57–63: `ionic_currents`.** These are the three conductance × driving force terms. Two things to notice:
- **m³h** and **n⁴** model one channel as several independent gates that must all be open at once. Sodium needs three m gates open and the h gate open; potassium needs four n gates open.
- The driving force (V − E_Na) is why the peak can't pass +50 mV, which ties back to your Q4 answer. This function is separate because **the extracellular waveform will be built from these currents** next.

**Lines 66–76: `hh_rhs`.** This is the whole model: four equations giving dV/dt, dm/dt, dh/dt and dn/dt. The V line is C·dV/dt = I_ext − I_Na − I_K − I_L. The three gate lines all follow the same rule: dx/dt = α(1 − x) − βx. It takes `t` as an input because the injected current can change over time.

**Lines 79–90: the integrators.**
- `euler_step` uses one slope, measured at the start of the step.
- `rk4_step` measures four slopes: at the start (k1), twice at the midpoint (k2 uses k1 to get there, k3 uses k2), and at the end (k4 uses k3). It then averages them with weights 1:2:2:1. That averaging cancels error terms up to dt⁴.
- Both are generic: they take any `f(t, y)`, so nothing in them is specific to HH.

**Lines 93–101: input currents.** `pulse` returns a *function*: you set the pulse up once, and the integrator can then ask for the current at any time t, including the half-steps RK4 uses.

**Lines 104–121: `simulate`.** It picks the step method, builds the time grid, and stores every state in an (n_steps + 1) × 4 array (column 0 is V). It then loops, each new state computed from the previous one. The inner `f` "bakes in" the chosen current, so the step functions only ever see `f(t, y)`.

**Lines 124–127: `count_spikes`.** It marks each sample as above or below 0 mV and counts the places where one sample is below and the next is above (`~above[:-1] & above[1:]`). A spike is one upward crossing, however long it stays above.

## Walkthrough of [test_hh.py](tests/test_hh.py)
Each test is one check from CLAUDE.md. The cleverest is `_error_ratio`: it has **no exact solution to compare against**.
- If the error is about C·dtᵖ, then (run at dt − run at dt/2) shrinks by 2ᵖ each time dt is halved.
- So it compares three runs at dt, dt/2 and dt/4.
- The `[::2]` and `[::4]` slices line the finer runs up with the coarse run's time points.
- It starts the cell at −50 mV with no pulse. A pulse switches on suddenly, and that jump would spoil RK4's dt⁴ behavior.

## Your turn: explain these back
1. Why does starting the cell at `steady_state(-65)` matter? What would the first few ms look like if we started with m = h = n = 0.5?
2. In `_error_ratio`, why would a sudden current pulse spoil the dt⁴ behavior?

**Commit reminder:** five files are new or changed: `spikesort/`, `tests/`, `requirements.txt`, `pytest.ini` and `.gitignore`. When you're ready, commit them with a message in your own words. Next comes the extracellular waveform, which is where you choose between 1/r and 1/r².

def ionic_currents(y):
    """Sodium, potassium and leak currents (outward positive) for state y."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na = G_NA * m**3 * h * (v - E_NA)
    i_k = G_K * n**4 * (v - E_K)
    i_l = G_L * (v - E_L)
    return i_na, i_k, i_l


def hh_rhs(t, y, i_ext):
    """dy/dt for the HH equations; i_ext is a function of time giving injected current."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na, i_k, i_l = ionic_currents(y)
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = rates(v)

    dv = (i_ext(t) - i_na - i_k - i_l) / C_M
    dm = alpha_m * (1.0 - m) - beta_m * m

"""Hodgkin-Huxley model of one patch of membrane, with hand-written integrators.

Units: time in ms, voltage in mV, current density in uA/cm^2,
conductance in mS/cm^2, capacitance in uF/cm^2.

The state is a length-4 array y = [V, m, h, n].
"""

import math

import numpy as np

# Classic HH parameters (squid axon, 6.3 C), shifted so rest is near -65 mV.
C_M = 1.0       # membrane capacitance
G_NA = 120.0    # max sodium conductance
G_K = 36.0      # max potassium conductance
G_L = 0.3       # leak conductance
E_NA = 50.0     # sodium reversal potential
E_K = -77.0     # potassium reversal potential
E_L = -54.387   # leak reversal, chosen so the resting potential is -65 mV
V_REST = -65.0


def _x_over_1_minus_exp(x, k):
    """Return x / (1 - exp(-x / k)), using its limit k when x is near 0.

    alpha_m and alpha_n have this form; plugging in x = 0 directly would
    divide 0 by 0.
    """
    if abs(x) < 1e-6:
        return k
    return x / (1.0 - math.exp(-x / k))


def rates(v):
    """Opening (alpha) and closing (beta) rates of the m, h, n gates at voltage v, in 1/ms."""
    alpha_m = 0.1 * _x_over_1_minus_exp(v + 40.0, 10.0)
    beta_m = 4.0 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 18.0)
    alpha_h = 0.07 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 20.0)
    beta_h = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-(v + 35.0) / 10.0))
    alpha_n = 0.01 * _x_over_1_minus_exp(v + 55.0, 10.0)
    beta_n = 0.125 * math.exp(-(v + 65.0) / 80.0)
    return alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n


def steady_state(v):
    """State [v, m, h, n] with every gate at its equilibrium value for a fixed v."""
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = rates(v)
    m = alpha_m / (alpha_m + beta_m)
    h = alpha_h / (alpha_h + beta_h)
    n = alpha_n / (alpha_n + beta_n)
    return np.array([v, m, h, n])


def ionic_currents(y):
    """Sodium, potassium and leak currents (outward positive) for state y."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na = G_NA * m**3 * h * (v - E_NA)
    i_k = G_K * n**4 * (v - E_K)
    i_l = G_L * (v - E_L)
    return i_na, i_k, i_l


def hh_rhs(t, y, i_ext):
    """dy/dt for the HH equations; i_ext is a function of time giving injected current."""
    v, m, h, n = y
    i_na, i_k, i_l = ionic_currents(y)
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = rates(v)

    dv = (i_ext(t) - i_na - i_k - i_l) / C_M
    dm = alpha_m * (1.0 - m) - beta_m * m
    dh = alpha_h * (1.0 - h) - beta_h * h
    dn = alpha_n * (1.0 - n) - beta_n * n
    return np.array([dv, dm, dh, dn])


def euler_step(f, t, y, dt):
    """One forward-Euler step: follow the slope at the start for the whole step."""
    return y + dt * f(t, y)


def rk4_step(f, t, y, dt):
    """One classical Runge-Kutta (RK4) step: a weighted average of four slopes."""
    k1 = f(t, y)
    k2 = f(t + dt / 2, y + dt / 2 * k1)
    k3 = f(t + dt / 2, y + dt / 2 * k2)
    k4 = f(t + dt, y + dt * k3)
    return y + dt / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)


def no_current(t):
    return 0.0


def pulse(start, duration, amplitude):
    """Current that is `amplitude` for start <= t < start + duration, else 0."""
    def i_ext(t):
        return amplitude if start <= t < start + duration else 0.0
    return i_ext

    """Integrate the HH equations from t = 0 to t_max.

    Returns (t, y): t has shape (n_steps + 1,), y has shape (n_steps + 1, 4)
    with columns V, m, h, n. Starts at rest unless y0 is given.
    """
    step = {"rk4": rk4_step, "euler": euler_step}[method]
    n_steps = int(round(t_max / dt))
    t = np.arange(n_steps + 1) * dt

    above = v >= threshold

"""Small checks for each function Tara writes, run before the whole-model checks in test_hh.py.

Run one group at a time, e.g.:  .venv/bin/pytest -v -k ionic
"""

import numpy as np
import pytest

from spikesort import hh


# --- ionic_currents ---------------------------------------------------------

def test_ionic_all_gates_open_at_0_mv():
    # Every gate open, V = 0: each current is just g_max * (0 - E).
    i_na, i_k, i_l = hh.ionic_currents(np.array([0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))
    assert i_na == pytest.approx(-6000.0)    # 120 * (0 - 50): inward, so negative
    assert i_k == pytest.approx(2772.0)      # 36 * (0 + 77): outward, so positive
    assert i_l == pytest.approx(16.3161)     # 0.3 * (0 + 54.387)


def test_ionic_gate_powers():
    # Gates at 0.5 test the m^3 h and n^4 powers.
    i_na, i_k, i_l = hh.ionic_currents(np.array([-65.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]))
    assert i_na == pytest.approx(-862.5)     # 120 * 0.5^3 * 0.5 * (-115)
    assert i_k == pytest.approx(27.0)        # 36 * 0.5^4 * 12
    assert i_l == pytest.approx(-3.1839)     # 0.3 * (-65 + 54.387)


def test_ionic_currents_cancel_at_rest():
    # At rest the three currents balance, which is what makes it rest.
    total = sum(hh.ionic_currents(hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST)))
    assert abs(total) < 0.01


# --- hh_rhs -----------------------------------------------------------------

def test_rhs_is_zero_at_rest():
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(0.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), hh.no_current)
    assert dy.shape == (4,)
    assert np.allclose(dy, 0.0, atol=0.01)


def test_rhs_injected_current_drives_v_only():
    # 10 uA/cm^2 into a cell at rest: dV/dt = 10 / C_M, gates not yet moving.
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(0.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), lambda t: 10.0)
    assert dy[0] == pytest.approx(10.0, abs=0.01)
    assert np.allclose(dy[1:], 0.0, atol=1e-9)


def test_rhs_uses_the_time_argument():
    # Current equal to t, evaluated at t = 3: dV/dt should be about 3.
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(3.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), lambda t: t)
    assert dy[0] == pytest.approx(3.0, abs=0.01)


def test_rhs_gate_equations():
    # m = 0 and n = 0: all gates closed, so dm/dt = alpha_m, dn/dt = alpha_n.
    # h = 1: all open, so dh/dt = -beta_h.
    alpha_m, beta_m, alpha_h, beta_h, alpha_n, beta_n = hh.rates(-65.0)
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(0.0, np.array([-65.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), hh.no_current)
    assert dy[1] == pytest.approx(alpha_m)
    assert dy[2] == pytest.approx(-beta_h)
    assert dy[3] == pytest.approx(alpha_n)


# --- rk4_step ---------------------------------------------------------------

def test_rk4_exponential_one_step():
    # dy/dt = y from y = 1. One RK4 step matches the Taylor series of e^dt
    # through dt^4: 1 + dt + dt^2/2 + dt^3/6 + dt^4/24.
    dt = 0.1

Good call, since the course grades what you can explain. In [hh.py](spikesort/hh.py), these three functions are now stubs that raise `NotImplementedError`, each marked `TODO (Tara)`:
- `ionic_currents`

You did see my version in the earlier walkthrough, so write these **without scrolling up**. It's the same test you'll face on Dec 3.

**Tests:**
- I added [test_hh_parts.py](tests/test_hh_parts.py) with 10 small tests, one group per function, so you get feedback one piece at a time.
- The 7 whole-model tests in `test_hh.py` stay as your final check.
- Right now all 17 fail on the stubs. I confirmed they all pass on a correct version kept outside your project, so when one fails, the problem is in your code, not the test.

## How to write each one

Run the commands from the project folder, `~/dev/spike-sorting`.

### Step 1: `ionic_currents(y)`
- Unpack the state: `v, m, h, n = y`.
- Each current = maximum conductance × fraction of channels open × driving force.
  - The fraction open for sodium involves m and h; for potassium, only n. The leak has no gates.
  - What powers go on the gates? Look back at your gate explanations.
  - The driving force is (V − E) for that ion. Use the constants at the top of the file, such as `G_NA` and `E_NA`.
- Return all three currents as a tuple.

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v -k ionic
```

If `test_ionic_all_gates_open_at_0_mv` fails on the sign, think about which way current flows when V < E_Na.

### Step 2: `hh_rhs(t, y, i_ext)`
- **dV/dt:** from C·dV/dt = (injected current) − (the three ionic currents). Remember that `i_ext` is a *function*, so how do you get the current at this moment?
- **dm/dt, dh/dt, dn/dt:** all three use the same rule. Get the six rates from `rates(v)`, then write each as (rate of closed gates opening) − (rate of open gates closing). Which fraction of gates is closed?
- Return all four values as one numpy array, in the order V, m, h, n.

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v -k rhs
```

### Step 3: `rk4_step(f, t, y, dt)`
Use `euler_step` as your template, since it has the same inputs and output. You need four slopes, each one a call to `f`:
1. **k1:** at the start of the step.
2. **k2:** at the midpoint in time, using k1 to estimate y there.
3. **k3:** at the midpoint again, this time using k2.
4. **k4:** at the end of the step, using k3.

Then combine them with weights 1, 2, 2, 1.

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v -k rk4
```

`test_rk4_exact_for_cubic_in_time` only passes if every slope is evaluated at the right *time*, so it catches a missing `t + dt/2`.

### Step 4: everything
```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v
```

The whole-model tests then check rest, one spike, gates within [0, 1], convergence, and the 4th-order versus 1st-order error ratios.

Write each function and run its tests. When a test fails, paste the output here and we'll work out the cause together before changing anything. Once all 17 pass, tell me and I'll review your code line by line.

content.text:
Here's a way to think it through. I'll stop short of the actual code.

## 1. Start with what goes in and what comes out
- **In:** `y`, the current state of the cell, an array of four numbers `[V, m, h, n]`.
- **Out:** three numbers, `(i_na, i_k, i_l)`, the current carried by each type of channel *right now*.

So the function is a snapshot: "given this voltage and these gates, how much current flows?" There's no time and no change in it yet. That comes in `hh_rhs`.

## 2. Write the physics in words, for one ion
Every current in HH follows **Ohm's law**: current = conductance × voltage. The two parts:
- **Conductance:** how easy it is for this ion to cross the membrane right now. That's the *maximum* conductance (all channels open) times the *fraction of channels open*.
- **Voltage that drives it:** not V itself but (V − E). At V = E, the ion's concentration gradient and the voltage balance exactly, so no net current flows.

So, for each ion: **current = maximum conductance × fraction open × (V − E)**.

## 3. Work out "fraction open" for each channel
This is the only part that differs between the three currents, and the fact you need is from your Q1 answers:
- **Sodium** has two kinds of gates. HH modeled a channel as conducting only when *several independent* gates are open at once. If one gate is open with probability m, what's the probability that 3 independent m gates are all open? Then the h gate must *also* be open. Combine those.
- **Potassium** has only one kind of gate, n, and HH used 4 of them. Same reasoning.
- **Leak** has no gates. What's its "fraction open"?

## 4. Check the sign before you code
The file says **outward is positive**. Check your formula with one case: at V = −65 mV, sodium's (V − E_Na) = (−65 − 50) = −115, which is negative, meaning inward. Is that right physically? Does Na⁺ flow into or out of the cell at rest? If your formula gives the right sign here without you adding any minus signs, it's correct.

## 5. Translate to Python
Three details trip people up:
- **Unpacking:** `v, m, h, n = y` gives you four named variables from the array.
- **Powers:** in Python, "x cubed" is `x ** 3`. Don't use `x ^ 3`. In Python, `^` means something unrelated, so it gives wrong numbers silently instead of raising an error.
- **Constants:** use the names at the top of the file (`G_NA`, `E_NA`, `G_K`, `E_K`, `G_L`, `E_L`), not typed-in numbers. Then if you change a parameter later, it changes everywhere.

## 6. Check by hand, then with the tests
Before running pytest, plug in the first test case yourself: V = 0 with every gate open (m = h = n = 1). What should each of the three currents be? Work it out on paper, then run:

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v -k ionic
```

If your paper answer and the test's expected numbers (−6000, 2772, 16.3161) agree, you understand the formula. If the code then fails, the mistake is in the translation to Python, not the physics.

**Before you write any code:** tell me your answer to the step 3 questions, the "fraction open" for sodium, potassium and leak, written as math. Once those are right, the function itself is about four lines.

def ionic_currents(y):
    """Sodium, potassium and leak currents (outward positive) for state y.

    Returns (i_na, i_k, i_l). Each is conductance x driving force.
    """
    V, m, h, n = y
    i_na = G_NA * (m**3 * h) * (V - E_NA)
    i_k = G_K * (n**4) * (V - E_K)
    i_l = G_L * (V - E_L)
    return (i_na, i_k, i_l)


def hh_rhs(t, y, i_ext):
    """dy/dt for the HH equations; i_ext is a function of time giving injected current.

    Returns np.array([dV/dt, dm/dt, dh/dt, dn/dt]).
    """
    i_na, i_k, i_l = ionic_currents(y)
    I = i_ext(t)
    dVdt = (I - i_na - i_k - i_l)/C_M

    raise NotImplementedError
</pasted_content id="dbc0">

# Spike sorting project — context for Claude Code

This is my final project for 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026). I work on it alone, with you as collaborator. The course grades whether I *learn* the science and the computation, not just whether the code works. Read the "How to work with me" section before doing anything.

## The project in one paragraph

I simulate extracellular brain recordings where the true spike times are known, then sort them with a spike sorter I write myself, to measure how many neurons a single electrode can reliably tell apart. The final product is an interactive web app.

**Scientific question:** How many distinct neurons can be reliably separated from a single electrode's signal, and how do noise level, waveform similarity and firing rate limit that number?

You already have them: **the gate variable itself is the fraction open.**

- `m` is the fraction of m gates that are open at this moment. It's always between 0 and 1. That's also why the gates had to stay in [0, 1] in your Q4 answer.
- Every gate is either open or closed, so the fraction **closed is `1 - m`**.
- The same goes for h and n: `h` open and `1 - h` closed, `n` open and `1 - n` closed.

You've already unpacked `m`, `h` and `n` on line 72, so you have everything you need.

**Putting it together for one gate:**
- Gates **open** at rate α, but only closed gates can open, so the flow into "open" is α × (fraction closed).
- Gates **close** at rate β, but only open gates can close, so the flow out of "open" is β × (fraction open).
- The net change in the fraction open is the flow in minus the flow out.

**Where α and β come from:** you haven't called `rates` yet. It takes the voltage and returns six numbers in this order: α_m, β_m, α_h, β_h, α_n, β_n. You'll need to unpack them into names, the same way you unpacked `y`.

**To check your thinking**, look at `steady_state` in the same file. It sets each gate to α / (α + β). That's the value where your dm/dt would be exactly 0, because opening and closing balance. Plug m = α/(α+β) into your expression and check that it gives 0. If it does, your formula is right.

"""Small checks for each function Tara writes, run before the whole-model checks in test_hh.py.

Run one group at a time, e.g.:  .venv/bin/pytest -v -k ionic
"""

import numpy as np
import pytest

from spikesort import hh


# --- ionic_currents ---------------------------------------------------------

def test_ionic_all_gates_open_at_0_mv():
    # Every gate open, V = 0: each current is just g_max * (0 - E).
    i_na, i_k, i_l = hh.ionic_currents(np.array([0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))
    assert i_na == pytest.approx(-6000.0)    # 120 * (0 - 50): inward, so negative
    assert i_k == pytest.approx(2772.0)      # 36 * (0 + 77): outward, so positive
    assert i_l == pytest.approx(16.3161)     # 0.3 * (0 + 54.387)


def test_ionic_gate_powers():
    # Gates at 0.5 test the m^3 h and n^4 powers.
    i_na, i_k, i_l = hh.ionic_currents(np.array([-65.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]))
    assert i_na == pytest.approx(-862.5)     # 120 * 0.5^3 * 0.5 * (-115)
    assert i_k == pytest.approx(27.0)        # 36 * 0.5^4 * 12
    assert i_l == pytest.approx(-3.1839)     # 0.3 * (-65 + 54.387)


def test_ionic_currents_cancel_at_rest():
    # At rest the three currents balance, which is what makes it rest.
    total = sum(hh.ionic_currents(hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST)))
    assert abs(total) < 0.01


# --- hh_rhs -----------------------------------------------------------------

def test_rhs_is_zero_at_rest():
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(0.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), hh.no_current)
    assert dy.shape == (4,)
    assert np.allclose(dy, 0.0, atol=0.01)


def test_rhs_injected_current_drives_v_only():
    # 10 uA/cm^2 into a cell at rest: dV/dt = 10 / C_M, gates not yet moving.
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(0.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), lambda t: 10.0)
    assert dy[0] == pytest.approx(10.0, abs=0.01)
    assert np.allclose(dy[1:], 0.0, atol=1e-9)


def test_rhs_uses_the_time_argument():
    # Current equal to t, evaluated at t = 3: dV/dt should be about 3.
    dy = hh.hh_rhs(3.0, hh.steady_state(hh.V_REST), lambda t: t)

Before you write it, check your understanding of the idea:
- Euler takes **one** slope, from the start of the step, and walks the whole step along it.

  4. **k4:** go back to the start, walk a **full** step along k3, and measure the slope at `t + dt`.
  5. Take the step from `y` using the average slope (k1 + 2·k2 + 2·k3 + k4) / 6.

That's not quite it. k2 and k3 aren't more accurate than k1 and k4. Each is just the slope at a different *place*. The weights come from what the step is actually doing.

**What the step computes:** to move from y(t) to y(t + dt), you need the area under the slope curve over the step:

$$y(t+dt) = y(t) + \int_t^{t+dt} \text{slope}\;ds$$

**Simpson's rule** estimates that area from the slope at the start, middle and end:

$$\int \approx \frac{dt}{6}\big(\text{start} + 4\cdot\text{middle} + \text{end}\big)$$

It fits a parabola through those three points, and for a parabola the area comes out with exactly these weights. The middle point gets a weight of 4 because it sits closest to all the area, not because its value is more trustworthy.

**RK4 is Simpson's rule with two estimates of the middle slope**, k2 and k3. Neither is exact, so RK4 splits the 4 between them: 1 + **2 + 2** + 1, over 6. Averaging the two midpoint estimates cancels some of each one's error, and that's where RK4's 4th order comes from.

To check you've got it, say it back in one sentence: *what is RK4 really estimating, and where does the 1-2-2-1 come from?*

content.text:
Start from `euler_step`, which you already have:

```python
return y + dt * f(t, y)
```

`f(t, y)` is just "the slope at time t, at state y." Euler takes one slope and walks the full `dt` along it.

**Hint 1: name the slopes.** RK4 needs four slopes, so store each one in its own variable. The first is exactly Euler's slope:

```python
k1 = f(t, y)
```

**Hint 2: each later slope is `f` called at a new time and a new state.** For k2, you need two things:
- **Time:** halfway through the step. What's that in terms of `t` and `dt`?
- **State:** where you'd be if you walked *half* a step along k1. This has the same shape as Euler's update, `y + (something) * k1`, but with half the step size.

**Hint 3: k3 and k4 follow the same pattern.** They just use a different slope to walk along and a different step size:

| | time | walk along | how far |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| k2 | midpoint | k1 | half a step |
| k3 | midpoint | ? | half a step |
| k4 | end of step | ? | ? |

Fill in the ?s from your own explanation: "the middle sampled twice," and the end of the step is reached using the second midpoint estimate.

**Hint 4: the final line looks like Euler's.** It's `y + dt * (slope)`, where the slope is now the 1-2-2-1 weighted average you described.

**A common mistake:** k3 and k4 always start walking from **`y`**, the start of the step, not from where the previous slope ended up. Every probe is "start at y, walk some distance along some slope."

Write it, then run:
```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -v -k rk4
```

If `test_rk4_exact_for_cubic_in_time` fails while the other two pass, check the *times* you pass to `f`.

# Spike sorting project — context for Claude Code

This is my final project for 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026). I work on it alone, with you as collaborator. The course grades whether I *learn* the science and the computation, not just whether the code works. Read the "How to work with me" section before doing anything.

## The project in one paragraph

I simulate extracellular brain recordings where the true spike times are known, then sort them with a spike sorter I write myself, to measure how many neurons a single electrode can reliably tell apart. The final product is an interactive web app.

**Scientific question:** How many distinct neurons can be reliably separated from a single electrode's signal, and how do noise level, waveform similarity and firing rate limit that number?

**Inspiring paper:** Quian Quiroga, Nadasdy & Ben-Shaul (2004), *Unsupervised spike detection and sorting with wavelets and superparamagnetic clustering*, Neural Computation (PDF in `papers/`).
**Related:** Pedreira et al. (2012), *How many neurons can we see with current spike sorting algorithms?*; Trautmann et al. (2019), sorting vs. unsorted threshold crossings (optional extension).
**Data:** none — everything is simulated, so ground truth is exact.

## Pipeline

1. **Simulator**
   - Spike trains: Poisson firing with a refractory period (~2 ms).
   - Waveforms: one Hodgkin–Huxley action potential (my own ODE integrator, e.g. RK4), converted to an extracellular waveform (tracks membrane current, not voltage), scaled by each neuron's distance from the electrode.
   - Recording: waveforms placed at spike times, summed, plus background noise (aim for realistic background from many distant neurons, not only white noise).
   - Output: voltage trace + answer key of true spike times and identities.
2. **Sorter (all core steps written by me, from scratch)**
   - Bandpass filter, zero-phase; band is a parameter, default 300–6000 Hz (matches the paper).
   - Negative-only threshold detection: x < −4σ, with robust noise estimate σ = median(|x|) / 0.6745, plus a dead time after each detection.
   - Align detected spikes on their trough.
   - Multilevel Haar wavelet transform; select coefficients by deviation from normality (KS test).
   - PCA features as a baseline for comparison.
   - Gaussian mixture model fitted by EM; number of neurons chosen by BIC (lowest BIC wins).
   - Scoring: match sorted spikes to true spikes within a fixed time window.
3. **Web app:** sliders for number of neurons, noise, waveform similarity, firing rate; panels for raw trace with sorted spikes, feature space, cluster waveforms, accuracy vs. ground truth; a sweep view of neurons recovered vs. neurons present.

## Differences from Quiroga et al. (2004)

Full write-up (paper vs. us, why, what it changes) lives in the README. Don't drift back to the paper's method on these:

1. **Filter band:** default 300–6000 Hz like the paper, but exposed as a parameter. f_rms (and so Rice's prediction) depends on the band.
2. **Polarity:** paper detects positive peaks; HH extracellular spikes are negative first, so we use a negative-only threshold (one-sided, mirror of the paper).
3. **Clustering:** GMM + EM with BIC instead of superparamagnetic clustering. GMM shares K-means' preference for compact Gaussian clusters, so compare against the paper's K-means result; a narrow wavelet advantage is a finding, not a bug.
4. **Waveforms:** HH-derived instead of real recorded shapes (check spike width ~1 ms; apply temperature correction if too slow). Shape variety via a small precomputed library of HH parameter sets plus distance-dependent smoothing (planned Week 5; Week 4 uses amplitude-only differences). Background noise from many distant neurons' spikes, like the paper.

## Other decisions

- **Libraries only for plumbing** (arrays, plotting, possibly the filter design). The course rejects "one library call fed into the next." Detection, Haar transform, coefficient selection, EM, BIC and scoring are mine.
- **Detection false-positive checks (one-sided, corrected Oct 30).** 1 − Φ(4) ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ is a *per-sample* probability. After filtering, neighboring samples are correlated, so one noise bump spans several samples but counts as one detection. Therefore:
  - Fraction of noise *samples* below −4σ should match 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ (white or filtered, with σ measured after filtering).
  - Detections per sample should match 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ only on **white** noise.
  - On **filtered** noise, detections per second should match Rice's formula for one-sided crossings: ≈ f_rms × exp(−u²/2) at u = 4, with f_rms computed from my filter's actual frequency response (ideal 300–6000 Hz band: f_rms ≈ 3.6 kHz → ≈ 1.2 false detections/s). Approximate because the signal is sampled.
- **Possible GMM stress test:** a bursting neuron (shrinking amplitude stretches its cluster) to see whether GMM wrongly splits it.

## Checks the project must pass

- Ground truth scoring: detection rate, false positives, assignment accuracy.
- Detection-rate checks above (one-sided exceedance fraction, white-noise detections, Rice's formula on filtered noise).
- Spike width of the HH-derived extracellular waveform is close to ~1 ms.
- Robust σ recovers true σ on pure noise and stays accurate as firing rate rises, while plain std overestimates.
- Two very different neurons, no noise → perfect sorting.
- Haar transform inverts exactly; hand-computed 8-sample example matches code.
- EM recovers known parameters of a synthetic Gaussian mixture; log-likelihood rises every iteration.
- Published behavior: wavelets match or beat PCA as sorting gets harder, compared against the paper's K-means result (Quiroga 2004); neurons recovered level off as more are added (Pedreira 2012).
- Refractory violations (<2 ms intervals) near zero for correct units, high for merged ones.
- With a fixed random seed, the app reproduces offline script results.

## Roadmap and course deadlines

Full week-by-week plan with action items: see `ROADMAP.md`.

| Week | Dates | Phase | Course deadline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Oct 8–14 | Simulate one neuron (HH, waveform, spike trains) | Proposal feedback Oct 9 |
| 2 | Oct 15–21 | Full recording, filtering, detection | Journal checkpoint 1 — Oct 21 |
| 3 | Oct 22–30 | Alignment, Haar features, PCA baseline | Journal checkpoint 2 — Oct 30 |
| 4 | Oct 31–Nov 6 | EM-GMM, BIC, scoring, first end-to-end sort | TA check-ins open Nov 4 |
| 5 | Nov 7–13 | Parameter sweeps; answer the question | TA check-in by Nov 13 |
| 6 | Nov 14–20 | Web app v1, deployed; README draft | App live + checkpoint 3 — Nov 20 |
| 7 | Nov 21–27 | Fixes; optional sorted-vs-unsorted extension | Thanksgiving Break |
| 8 | Nov 28–Dec 1 | README, ≤5-min video, demo prep | Final app/code/video + demo day — Dec 1 |
| — | Dec 3 | — | Closed, on-paper project assessment |

**Current status:** Re-planned Nov 10, see ROADMAP.md; HH integrator in progress.

## How to work with me

My session logs are graded as a build journal. The graders look for learning, steady work, and checking — so:

- **Teach before building.** When we start a new concept (filtering, wavelets, EM, Rice's formula…), explain it first, then quiz me and let me explain it back before writing code.
- **Explain code you write.** After writing anything non-trivial, walk me through what it does and why. Expect me to ask "why?" often.
- **Debug with me, don't just fix.** When something breaks, help me form hypotheses and test them rather than silently patching it.
- **Always tie work to a check.** New code should come with a test or a comparison against one of the checks above.
- **Keep scope small.** Get the smallest version working and checked before adding features.
- **Don't write my commit messages** — remind me to write them in my own words.
- **Flag deviations.** If something we do departs from the paper or this file, say so and suggest recording it (README or here).
- **Prepare me for Dec 3.** I must be able to explain, without notes: the extracellular spike shape and distance scaling; HH variables and my integrator; why 300–6000 Hz and what changing the band does; where 0.6745 comes from; why a negative-only threshold; the one-sided 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ derivation, why filtered noise gives fewer detections, and Rice's prediction; each of the four differences from Quiroga et al. and what it costs; a Haar transform by hand; why non-Gaussian coefficients are chosen; EM steps, monotone likelihood, and what BIC trades off; scoring and refractory violations; my answer with its numbers; and what the simulation leaves out.
